item.title: Synergizing LLMs and Formal Methods for Neural-Symbolic Reasoning
item.dc:creator: Jin Song Dong
item.description: Presenting a neural-symbolic paradigm in which LLMs propose candidate artifacts and formal methods gate acceptance with machine-checkable certificates.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, the rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has marked a transformative shift in the landscape of artificial intelligence and many of its applications: software engineering,12 finance,28 healthcare,13 and legal,14 among others. Top LLMs, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek, have demonstrated impressive capabilities in multimodal understanding, generation, coding, task execution, and reasoning. Leveraging these capabilities, agentic LLMs can plan, take actions, and use feedback loops with memory to achieve goals autonomously.

Key Insights

  • LLMs can lower the entry barrier to formal methods (FM) by helping users express informal requirements, generate candidate artifacts, and interact with formal tools.

  • LLMs explore the design space by proposing candidate artifacts, while FM back ends enforce a certificate-based acceptance boundary grounded in explicit assurance targets.

  • A promising direction is to unify these paradigms by using LLMs for generation and interaction, while relying on FM to enforce correctness and interpretability.

  • The aim of an LLM+FM architecture is not merely to produce better average outputs, but to make success and failure observable through formal feedback, with completion gated by a certificate.

Despite these advances, LLM reasoning suffers from a fundamental limitation: the tendency to produce factually incorrect or logically inconsistent yet plausible outputs, commonly termed hallucinations.11 This poses serious risks in high-stakes domains, where trustworthiness is critical. Importantly, this issue is not anomalous but rather mathematically inherent to the probabilistic objectives underlying LLM training. As an example, we asked the LLMs to solve a simple puzzle: In 318, only one digit is correct, and it is in the correct position. In 379, only one digit is correct, but it is in the wrong position. In 863, two digits are correct, but they are in the wrong positions. In 421, no digits are correct. What’s the correct combination of the three digits and their positions? Older models such as GPT 4.1, Gemini 2.5, Claude 4 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3, and Grok 3 gave wrong answers with believable thinking processes. Reasoning models, such as the “Thinking” or “Pro” modes, fared better but took minutes to respond. Small open source LLMs performed poorly and often fell into an infinite loop of reasoning. These models are constantly evolving—the latest versions of GPT, Gemini, and Claude all answered correctly (698). However, hallucinations persist, and theoretically cannot be eradicated by training better LLMs alone.26

Interestingly, we also asked Claude 4 to translate the puzzle into Z3’s SMT-LIB format, which Z3 solved correctly in 0.01 seconds on a laptop (MacBook Pro with M1 Pro). Z3 is a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver,7 offering rigorous reasoning complementary to the probabilistic nature of LLMs. More broadly, formal methods (FM) provide mathematically precise tools for trustworthy computing: SMT extends classical satisfiability to theories such as arithmetic, bit-vectors, arrays, datatypes, and uninterpreted functions; theorem proving derives valid formulas from axioms via proof calculi; and model checking systematically explores system states to detect property violations.

Compared to the uncertain and generative nature of LLMs, formal methods deliver rigorous correctness guarantees, but their adoption is limited by steep learning curves and high expertise requirements. A promising direction is to unify these paradigms by leveraging LLMs for generation and interaction while using formal methods to enforce correctness and interpretability.6,25

A Neural-Symbolic Reasoning Paradigm

Notable neural-symbolic AI methods.  A common early pattern in LLM-based formal reasoning is loosely coupled integration, where an LLM translates a problem into a formal language for a symbolic solver, and solver failures due to syntactic or semantic issues are fed back to the LLM for iterative refinement.2,19,21 In contrast, tightly integrated approaches embed neural reasoning directly into the formal reasoning loop. For example, LeanDojo employs retrieval-augmented premise selection based on the current proof state and an encoder-decoder transformer to propose the next proof tactic, enabling fine-grained neural-symbolic collaboration.27

Other tightly integrated paradigms include logical neural networks (LNNs), where neurons correspond to components of weighted logical formulas in a real-valued logic, yielding end-to-end differentiability, omnidirectional inference, and training-time enforcement of logical consistency.20 Scallop further advances this line through a neurosymbolic programming language and compiler that supports data- and computation-efficient training while delivering strong performance, interpretability, and generalization across diverse tasks.15 Beyond such architectures, directly integrating formal methods into the internal components of LLMs remains possible but prohibitively resource intensive. Our work instead adopts a practical and complementary strategy: constraining, checking, and guiding LLM outputs via external formal methods without requiring access to model internals. By formalizing the representations, constraints, and reasoning interfaces between LLMs and downstream systems, we ensure verifiability while enabling accessible deployment of reliability mechanisms in high-stakes applications.

Our paradigm.  Across integration styles, common neural-symbolic interaction themes emerge (Figure 1). To lower the entry barrier, natural language is used as input, with multiple LLM agents coordinated by an agentic task automation LLM that selects agents, interacts with users, and automates the workflow. Complex problems typically follow a “plan-execute” decomposition.12 The resulting gap between informal input and formal specifications is bridged by an autoformalization LLM, while a designing LLM converts underspecified prompts into high-level designs. Given the close link between formal methods and software engineering, many execution steps involve programming and are handled by a coding LLM. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies domain knowledge, including language syntax and semantics, and enables downstream applications. LLM agents interact with formal reasoning engines, including SMT solvers, theorem provers, and model checkers, whose reliable outputs provide high-quality feedback for repairing and refining autoformalized code.

Guidelines on architecture design.  An LLM+FM architecture should be selected from the assurance target outward, rather than from an LLM workflow inward. The aim is not merely better average outputs, but rather an architecture where success and failure are observable through formal feedback and where completion is gated by a certificate, that is, machine-checkable evidence produced by the FM back end (e.g., a localized conflict explanation, a violating execution trace, or an undischarged proof). This also future-proofs the design: LLM capabilities may change quickly, but the acceptance boundary is defined by certificates that can be validated independently of the LLM.

Design Rule 1 (Assurance target).  State the artifact that must be correct and the related properties that define correctness. Write the acceptance claim in the form “This output is acceptable because <property> holds for <artifact>.” If this claim cannot be stated precisely, later choices drift toward optimizing fluency or convenience rather than the intended notion of correctness.

Design Rule 2 (Back-end FM choice).  An FM back end should be chosen to match the property class and, more fundamentally, the domain of quantification. For constraint satisfiability and consistency questions that expect definitive outcomes (e.g., SAT/UNSAT), SMT-based back ends are most appropriate, as they determine logical formula satisfiability and can return unsat cores to localize conflicting constraints, providing constraint-level correctness. For behavioral and temporal properties, model checking is better suited, as it reasons exhaustively over transition systems, verifies whether all executions satisfy a temporal specification, and otherwise produces counterexample traces, with first-class support for safety, liveness, and fairness, yielding behavioral/temporal correctness. For refinement and high-assurance correctness, theorem proving and refinement checking adopt a proof-centric approach, generating and discharging proof obligations to certify that a system meets its specification by construction, providing semantic, unbounded correctness; when full certification is too costly, lighter-weight techniques such as type systems, abstract interpretation, or contract checking can offer faster but partial guarantees.

Design Rule 3 (LLM-FM interface).  After fixing the FM back end, define the contract between generation and validation by deciding what the LLM may propose (candidates, decompositions, repairs) and what the FM tool must return on failure. Treat formal failures as typed signals rather than generic “try again” events, so prompts and repair logic are organized around channels such as inconsistency, counterexample, or unsatisfied obligation. Finer-grained diagnostics typically shorten repair cycles and reduce silent failure, at the cost of tighter tool integration and more orchestrated iterations. A further trade-off is where human effort is spent: It can be front-loaded via structured inputs that reduce ambiguity, or back-loaded via flexible inputs plus more validation cycles and occasional interactive confirmation.

Design Rule 4 (Integration pattern).  Select a coupling pattern that matches the dominant failure mode and the task abstraction level. For decision/compliance settings (e.g., access-control policies, configuration constraints), consistency-guarded deliberation works well: Deliberate freely, but gate acceptance with a consistency checker that surfaces localized conflicts. For system-level behaviors (e.g., protocol workflows, safety controllers), counterexample-guided refinement is effective: Failed checks yield executions that drive targeted revisions, at the cost of repeated checking and occasional abstraction. For component synthesis (e.g., critical parsers and code), proof-obligation guided synthesis is effective: Obligations pinpoint repair targets, but require precise specifications and manageable proof burden. Patterns are often combined across layers; when both system- and code-level assurance are needed, certify the higher-level model or contracts first, then constrain and certify lower-level synthesis.

Design Rule 5 (Acceptance guard).  State explicitly the certificate that gates acceptance for the end-to-end system and what exactly it certifies. This operationalizes “good vs. bad” choices and makes trade-offs legible: Stronger certificates raise iteration cost and may narrow applicability, while lighter-weight certificates broaden scope but leave more residual uncertainty. In practice, designs are most robust when they align the architecture with the task abstraction level, treat FM as the correctness filter rather than an optional add-on, and keep a clean separation between candidate generation and certificate-based validation.

In summary, LLMs and FM will form a complementary and beneficial generate-validate loop in future applications: LLMs explore the design space by proposing candidate artifacts, while FM back ends enforce a certificate-based acceptance boundary grounded in explicit assurance targets. Formal failures verified by FM would become structured feedback that guides iterative refinement, aligning probabilistic generation with semantic guarantees. In the following sections, we will provide some examples of our neural-symbolic reasoning paradigm to demonstrate the different roles of LLMs and formal reasoning in a variety of application domains.

FM4LLM: Legal AI with LLM-SMT Integration

As our first case study, we show how formal reasoning enhances the reliability and consistency of LLM outputs in legal reasoning. While substantive rationality concerns fairness and morality, formal rationality demands logical adherence to the law. Existing legal LLMs, such as LawLLM,22 primarily rely on natural language processing and retrieval-augmented generation to reduce hallucinations, but still lack logically grounded and reliable reasoning.

Our approach,4 shown in Figure 2, addresses the above issue using SMT solving. Each statutory clause c is parsed into a typed rule Rule(c):=〈Actor,Action,Cond,Penalty〉, and compiled into a first-order implicationϕc:=∀x.Actor(x)∧Action(x)∧Cond(x)→Penalty(x). All articles form the static legal knowledge base K:={ϕc|c∈Statutes}. Given a case D, the Prosecutor and Attorney LLMs generate (FP,SP):=ProsecutorLLM(D),(FD,SD):=AttorneyLLM(D), where F are fact predicates and S are cited clauses. The autoformalization LLM acts neutrally and takes the evidence provided by the above two LLMs and generates SMT-LIB format formal code that Z3 can check. If Z3 reports unsatisfiable, we will extract the minimal unsatisfiable core, representing the simplest reason that causes logical inconsistency. The autoformalization LLM maps this core back to the original text and instructs the Prosecutor or Attorney LLM to drop the contradictory clauses, then asks Z3 to check for consistency again.

Example.  Consider the following real case: (Gong Qiang concerns a repeat narcotics offender) Defendant Gong Qiang received a WeChat message from Luo, requesting the purchase of 1,000 yuan worth of drugs. After receiving the 1,000 yuan transfer from Luo via WeChat, Gong Qiang delivered 2 grams of methamphetamine and six magu tablets to Luo at approximately 5:00 PM …

Taking the case information as input, the Prosecutor LLM (accusatory stance) extracts:

  • Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang (prior drug convictions), buyer Luo; public prosecution by Donghu District People’s Procuratorate

  • Acts: Sold 2g methamphetamine + 6 “magu” tablets for 1,000 RMB

  • Evidence: WeChat payment record, seized drugs, positive urine tests, confession

  • Aggravators: Repeat drug offender in five-year window; multiple prior administrative penalties

  • Statutory Law: [64, 65]; [347, 356]

On the other hand, the Attorney LLM (exculpatory stance) extracts:

  • Actors: Defendant Gong Qiang, buyer Luo; defense counsel appointed

  • Acts: Acknowledge sale but stress “very small quantity” and no wider circulation

  • Evidence: WeChat record, drug test, confession

  • Mitigators: Full confession, signed plea agreement, voluntary compensation and buyer’s understanding; prior sentence already served, limited social harm

  • Statutory Law: [64, 67]; [347, 356]

The autoformalization LLM analyzes the above results and further extracts the following facts and converts them into SMT-LIB format, then sends them to the Z3 solver together with the extracted rules and clauses:

  • Article 65: matched field { prior_sentence: True, reoffense_in_5_years: True }

  • Article 67: matched field { truthful_confession: True }

  • Article 347: matched fields {subject: person, action: traffic_narcotics, object: narcotics, intent: intentional}

Z3 evaluates the logical constraints and produces consistent results, which a judge LLM converts into a human-readable verdict of two years’ imprisonment and a 10,000 yuan fine, close to the ground truth of one year and two months with an 11,000 yuan penalty. This legally informed integration employs multiple role-specific LLM agents coordinated with an SMT solver to ensure logical consistency, leading to more realistic sentencing and the highest accuracy among state-of-the-art methods.4

LLM4FM: LLM Model-Checking Agent

LLMs can reduce the costly manual effort in formal methods. This case study presents a multi-LLM-agent framework that automates the full model-checking workflow. While model checking itself is automated once a formal model and properties are provided, its industrial adoption is hindered by the manual creation of models and specifications, which requires expertise in checker-specific modeling languages and temporal logics unfamiliar to most engineers.

Autoformalization is central to LLM-driven formal methods. Prior work has used LLMs to translate natural language into linear temporal logic (LTL) formulas9 and to synthesize or repair formal proofs,8 but these do not target system-level modeling. Our case study focuses on the Process Analysis Toolkit (PAT),23 which employs CSP#10 as the modeling language. The PAT-Agent framework29 (Figure 3) takes a natural language system description comprising system behavior and expected properties, translating the former into a formal model and the latter into requirements—properties with specified expected outcomes (i.e., expected to hold or not hold).

We introduce the following notation: Let LNL be the space of natural language descriptions, Π the planning representations, P the generation plans, M the PAT models, Q the user requirements, V PAT’s verification procedure, C the counterexample traces, and R the repair directives. With these notations, our pipeline is summarized by the four transformations:

T plan : L NL → Π → P ; T gen : P → M ; V : M × Q → { MATCH , MISMATCH } m × C ; T repair : M × C × R → M .

Our objective is to obtain a model M*∈M such that ∀(ϕ,o)∈Q:V(M*,ϕ)=o. In the first stage, a Planning LLM parses the system description to extract semantic elements such as constants, variables, actions, and guards, and produces a model-generation plan that defines the intended structure and includes placeholder annotations with explanatory comments to guide subsequent code synthesis. It also processes the user-specified requirements for the system (e.g., reachability and liveness requirements).

User studies show that PAT-Agent translates requirements with 99.6% accuracy across multiple projects. In rare cases, manual checks are still required, supported by optional checkpoints in PAT-Agent. In the second stage, a Coding LLM translates the model-generation plan into CSP# code, guided by formal syntax and semantics and a corpus of existing PAT models. In our experiments, Claude 3.7 Sonnet generates CSP# code with near-perfect syntax on the first attempt, with any minor issues resolved automatically through brief LLM interaction. Full semantic correctness cannot be guaranteed in an automated method, as it depends on user intent, but this issue can be mitigated by checking the generated model against the automatically formalized properties and expected outcomes using PAT. Assuming that the properties are formalized correctly and they sufficiently capture the user’s intent, model checking itself will largely resolve modeling inaccuracies. When mismatches occur, a model repair loop is triggered: PAT’s output, including counterexamples, guides a Repair Agent to identify and fix only the faulty code region rather than regenerating the entire model. In practice, three to four repair iterations typically suffice to satisfy all properties.

Example.  An electrical engineer describes the motor engine as follows:a

This process models a car’s motor. The engine can be turned on and off, the car can start and stop driving, the fuel is gradually consumed after driving, and it can be refueled.

The Planning LLM extracts and defines key constants, variables, and actions (e.g., carMotion, fuel, engineStatus, startDriving), assigning context-appropriate names and inferring implicit system logic using common sense. For example, it deduces that startDriving requires the engine to be on, the car to be stationary, sufficient fuel, and driver presence. The Coding LLM then instantiates this plan by filling in concrete model details, translating such inferred actions into:

[engineStatus == engineOn && carMotion == stop && (fuel > 0)
    && driver == inCar]
startDriving {carMotion = drive;} -> motor()

The code follows CSP# syntax [conditions] event_name data_operations -> next_process(), where guards specify enabling conditions and data operations define event effects, and it passes PAT’s syntax check on the first attempt. The Coding LLM also formalizes system requirements, for example, translating “the car should not be in driving mode without the key” into a reachability assertion, where the state driveWithoutKey is expected to be unreachable:

#define driveWithoutKey (carMotion==drive && key!=inCar);
#assert car reaches driveWithoutKey;     // Expects Invalid

However, verification results may show that the above state is reachable given the initial model generated by the Coding LLM. This issue, together with a counterexample trace composed of system states that lead to the error, is sent to the Repair Agent for a repair iteration, after which the above process is revised as follows to avoid the error:

[engineStatus == engineOn && carMotion == stop && (fuel > 0)
    && driver == inCar
&& key == inCar] startDriving {carMotion = drive;} -> motor()

Interestingly, this issue reflects a real-life situation in which a coauthor of this article kept the engine on and dropped off a passenger, who took the key, at a shopping mall. The author continued to drive the car to the office, only to realize he could not lock the car! With PAT-Agent, automakers can now verify their designs without the excuse of, “But we do not have formal methods engineers.”

They Are One: Trustworthy AI Coder

Some powerful integrations of neural-symbolic reasoning require the two parts to work hand in hand in each small step. This case study demonstrates an AI coder that combines LLMs, program refinement, and theorem proving into a hybrid system. LLMs have shown potent coding capabilities, and the latest ones have raised the bar to the project level—the user only needs to give a one-line prompt, and GPT 5 can build a fully functional website. However, the fundamental reliability problem remains: Is the code functionally correct with respect to user specifications?

Example.  We asked GPT 5 to write the following function: Generate a program that finds the square root of N within the error bound e.

GPT 5 produced the Python code below. However, the reader can check that the two lines after the for loop are incorrect, as there exist N and e such that abs(x_next - x) <= e, but abs(x_next⌃2 - N) > e, which violates the specification. Such issues prompted us to build a reliable AI coder,3 illustrated in Figure 4. To ensure correctness, we adopt the refinement calculus18 to derive code from first-order logic specifications via correctness-preserving transformations. A program is viewed as a predicate transformer, and refinement as logical implications between transformers. Starting from a pure specification Spec, the calculus incrementally replaces conjuncts and quantifiers with executable constructs, such as assignments, guards, loops, and nondeterministic choices using laws like assignment introduction, guard strengthening, and loop introduction, until only code remains. Traditionally, each refinement step requires human intervention:  selecting a refinement law whose side conditions hold, instantiating schema variables to produce a program fragment, and discharging the proof obligations (POs) ensuring Spec⊑Code. This manual workflow scales poorly for real-world systems, where large specifications may require hundreds of refinement steps. To address scalability, we integrate LLMs into the refinement loop. Given the current specification state Si, the LLM predicts a suitable refinement law, instantiates it to generate a candidate code fragment Ci, and emits the associated proof obligation (PO) induced by the refinement law. For example, the VC for an assignment, {P}x:=E{Q}, requires proving the logical implication P⇒Q[x↦E]. An automated theorem prover (ATP) attempts to discharge all POs. If all succeed, the refinement commits to Si+1. If any PO fails, the ATP produces the failing proof state (e.g., an unsatisfied VC or counterexample model), which is fed back to the LLM. The LLM may revise the code, select a different refinement rule, or backtrack to the last verified state. This yields a search-and-repair refinement process jointly guided by symbolic reasoning and neural generation.

def sqrt_w_err(N, e, max_iter=10000):
    if e <= 0 or N < 0:
        raise ValueError
    if N == 0: return 0.0
    x = N if N >= 1 else 1.0
    for _ in range(max_iter):
       x_next = 0.5 * (x + N / x)
       if (abs(x_next - x) <= e
           or abs(x_next^2 - N) <= e):
           return x_next
       x = x_next
    return x

Back to the square root example, our method generated the code below. Our code is guaranteed correct with respect to the proof obligations required by the refinement calculus in each step. Only one human input remains: This method requires the specification in first-order logic at the starting point, but not every programmer is knowledgeable in logic.

N, e = input()
x, y = 0, N+1
while y > x+e:
    if (x+y)/2*(x+y)/2 > N:
       y = (x+y)/2
    else: x = (x+y)/2

LLM-based autoformalization can mitigate this, as done in the previous case study, but the core issue remains: What if the translation is wrong? We argue that no perfect and fully automatic solution exists, as verification ultimately depends on correctness criteria defined by the user. In the experiment, our method improves the pass rate on popular datasets, such as HumanEval5 and EvalPlus,16 over the base LLM. That is, if the LLM becomes more intelligent, our method’s result will be improved on top of that. More importantly, unlike LLMs, whose pass rate decreases with more test cases, indicating that potential bugs still exist, our method’s pass rate is consistent regardless of test cases because programs are proven correct. Those that fail do so mainly because the theorem prover timed out, which, in turn, could be enhanced by LLMs.

Mitigating Autoformalization Risk

A common issue across LLM+FM paradigms is the translation from informal user intention to formal specification. We generally assume that the user sufficiently specifies their requirements in natural language and manually confirms the formal specification generated by the autoformalization module. Beyond syntax, the main risk is semantic under-specification: Natural language omits assumptions, scopes, and constraints, so an autoformalizer can produce a logically consistent but intent-misaligned specification that still passes solver checks and yields certificates for the wrong target. Robustness can be improved with typed intermediate representations and constrained decoding, where the LLM emits a type-checked schema compiled deterministically into the target formalism, and with semantic validation via round-trip paraphrases and automatically generated “should/should-not” scenarios checked against both the original intent and the formal solver.

A practical mitigation is N-version autoformalization: Generate multiple independent formalizations using different LLMs or prompt/decoding variants of the same LLM, and filter them with lightweight formal checks (well-formedness/type constraints, satisfiability and non-triviality, and consistency against fixed background constraints). Material disagreement in structure or consequences is treated as a high-risk signal and surfaced explicitly rather than being silently resolved. When appropriate, a router+specialists strategy (a system-level mixture of experts) can further reduce mismatch by dispatching inputs to domain- and logic-specific formalizers or templates, while keeping the same certificate-producing back end as the acceptance gate.

Finally, while certificate-producing back ends provide strong guarantees of logical validity, they do not eliminate epistemic uncertainty regarding specification fidelity. Formal methods act as verifiers of consistency, not arbiters of semantic truth. Bridging the informal-formal gap therefore remains an open research challenge, requiring improved interactive specification protocols, structure-aware validation, and human-in-the-loop confirmation mechanisms.

Conclusion and Future Work

This article presents a neural-symbolic paradigm in which LLMs propose candidate artifacts and formal methods gate acceptance with machine-checkable certificates. The three case studies illustrate this paradigm, but the key contribution is a reusable design view: Select from the assurance target outward, choose an FM back end for the property class, and use formal feedback to drive revision so errors become observable rather than implicit.

Beyond the case studies, the same paradigm applies to other integrations of LLMs and FM24 and applications in compliance analysis, protocol verification, cyber-physical safety, and synthesis of critical components. Recent progress around Lean further illustrates this opportunity. Mathlib17 shows how an extensive machine-checked library can support large-scale formalization and provide a strong foundation for later AI-assisted proof tools, while CSLib1 seeks to extend this effort to computer science concepts and verified code for AI-aided FM. Together, these projects suggest that shared formal libraries and reusable proof artifacts can help LLMs and formal methods achieve results beyond what either could readily do alone.

Future work will broaden these directions and further close the autoformalization gap via N-version translation (across models or prompt variants), router+specialists, typed intermediate representations, and scenario-based semantic validation.

item.title: In Software that Moves Money, the Model Never Holds the Pen
item.dc:creator: Dylan Merigaud
item.description: In software that moves money, a key decision involves which parts of the system a model may enter.
item.content:encoded:
Ledgerloop is an open source procure-to-pay workflow I built after almost two years as a forward-deployed engineer at a procurement fintech, where I turned enterprise clients’ approval rules into product configuration. When a vendor invoice arrives as a PDF, it gets matched against a purchase order, goes through an approval chain, and is reconciled into the accounting system. Writing it from scratch forced me to decide, component by component, whether a model was allowed to touch it.

I started from exact code and let a model in only where the input is fuzzy. That ordering matters for any software whose output someone will later have to defend, and money is the clearest case.

Two Answers to One Question

A language model samples. Ask it the same question twice and you may get two different answers; above a temperature of zero, that variation is by design. When the job is drafting text, nobody minds. When the job is deciding whether an invoice matches its purchase order, it disqualifies the model.

The question a controller or an auditor asks months later is simple: why was this bill paid? In ledgerloop, the answer is a function. The matching process lives in lib/matching.ts (commit 6af9fb1 on github.com/DylanMerigaud/ledgerloop). It compares quantities and unit prices line by line against a purchase order and a goods receipt, with a price tolerance of 1% to absorb rounding and currency conversion, and it returns one of three verdicts: clean, exception, or duplicate. Run it 1,000 times on the same inputs and you get the same verdict every time. When it is wrong, the bug has a line number.

The approval engine works the same way. The workflow is a graph of gates, each with a condition on the amount, the variance, the department, or the verdict, and the engine walks it. A bill posts only when every active gate has a human approval, and one rejection blocks everything after it. No model sits anywhere on that path. The project README states the rule in one sentence:

Everything else, matching, the workflow engine, reconciliation, is deterministic code, because a payment decision must be exact and repeatable, never a model’s guess.

None of this is new. Payment systems were built this way long before language models. What matters is that they stay built this way after a model is added.

Where the Model Belongs

Hold that line and the places where a model belongs become easy to see: they are the places where a deterministic rule would be brittle or impossible to write.

Reading a vendor’s PDF is the plainest example. Every supplier has its own invoice layout, and parsers built on regular expressions lose that race. A vision model reads the document into a structured invoice, the result is validated against a schema, and from there on code takes over.

Onboarding is another. In my previous job, setting up a new client meant an engineer reading their org chart and turning it into approval rules by hand: who signs what, above which amount. Mapping job titles to signing authority takes judgment, and real org data is messy, with a manager who left last month or two people who both look like the CEO. So an agent reads the HR system and proposes the workflow, with those problems flagged. Code assembles the proposal into a validated graph, and a person reviews and edits it in plain language before anything goes live. An edit that would produce an invalid graph is refused.

Investigating an exception is the last. In the demo data, invoice INV-2042 bills steel bar about 9% above its purchase order, and that number alone does not say whether the supplier raised its prices for a good reason or overcharged. That answer lives in notes, past invoices, and vendor history, and which of those matter depends on what you find along the way. This is the one open-ended agent on the operational path (src/mastra/agents/investigator.ts, commit 38f4f16). It chooses which records to read and writes a recommendation. A person makes the call.

These uses share a shape. The model works on unstructured input and hands a proposal to either code or a person. It never holds the pen on the outcome.

The Handoff Is Where the Engineering Goes

When the model can only propose, the human step becomes a part you have to design. The reviewer has to see what the agent concluded and why, in the place where they decide, or the review turns into a rubber stamp or a queue. In ledgerloop the paused bill shows the investigator’s recommendation next to the Approve and Reject buttons, and the run’s trace lists every record the agent opened on the way. The approver reads the case in one place and decides, and the decision stays with the person who is accountable for it.

A Default for Other Domains

Money makes the failure visible, but the reasoning carries to any system with an audit trail: access control, insurance claims, medical billing, anywhere someone may later ask why the system did what it did. I suggest a simple test for each component. If you would be uncomfortable answering that question with “the model thought so,” the component is code, and the model’s job is to prepare its input.

Most of my design time on ledgerloop went into deciding which parts of the system a model may enter. In software that moves money, getting that right leaves most of the system as boring, auditable code. I argued a shorter version of this on my site in July, and the ledgerloop source is public for anyone who wants to check where the line falls.

Dylan Merigaud is a software engineer based in Paris. He was a forward deployed engineer at the procurement fintech Pivot and built ledgerloop, an open source procure-to-pay workflow.

item.title: AI Agents Can’t Talk
item.dc:creator: Abhilash Pakalapati
item.description: Teams will continue to drown in token costs and unpredictable runtime behavior until we stop framing multi-agent design around the metaphor of human conversation.
item.content:encoded:
When software leaders hear that multi-agent systems are “talking to each other,” they typically picture an autonomous, real-time collaboration layer of agents negotiating, delegating, and reasoning in fluid conversation. The marketing narrative paints a compelling picture of decentralized digital workforces conducting rich dialogues to solve complex operational goals. But as engineering teams attempt to scale these architectures beyond controlled pilot environments into production environments, they hit a blunt reality: AI agents don’t talk. What looks like an organic exchange of intelligence is actually just a sequence of brittle, state-machine handoffs masquerading as dialogue.

At a fundamental architectural level, large language models (LLMs) are stateless text-completion functions. They possess no active transport mechanism, socket listener, or runtime memory to “hear” or “speak” continuously. When Agent A passes an output to Agent B, it is executing a standard request-response transaction across standard compute infrastructure. Agent A serializes its intermediate generation into a structured schema (often a raw JSON payload), transmits it across a middleware proxy or message broker, and Agent B unrolls that payload into a fresh context window. Calling this inter-agent communication misleads systems architects into applying conversational paradigms to what is fundamentally distributed remote procedure call (RPC) execution.

This conceptual misstep carries massive cost and performance consequences. In a human team, dialogue refines ideas through back-and-forth feedback. In an LLM-based system, dialogue expands token overhead exponentially. As detailed in my earlier post, “The Hidden Token Trap of Agent Orchestration,” when developers design multi-agent loops that rely on natural language negotiations to reach consensus, they force every participating agent to re-read and re-process the entire prior exchange with every single turn. A five-turn discussion between three worker agents does not yield deeper reasoning; it simply bloats the prompt payload, multiplies API inference fees, and introduces processing latency that renders real-time automation unusable.

The illusion of dialogue breaks down fastest inside the context window. In conversational multi-agent setups, every “turn” in the conversation appends the raw history of both agents into the next prompt generation. As task complexity grows, token consumption scales non-linearly. More critically, dumping uncurated message logs into downstream context windows triggers severe attention drift and compounding hallucinations. When agents consume unverified synthetic outputs from one another, they mirror the feedback-loop degradation identified in foundational research by Shumailov et al. on AI model collapse. Without deterministic verification boundaries between handoffs, message-passing turns multi-agent systems into quiet echo chambers of cascading failure.

To escape this trap, enterprise software architects must replace conversational abstractions with explicit state management. Rather than letting agents pass conversational threads back and forth, production architectures rely on central state stores, event buses, or key-value caches. Agent A finishes its sub-task, writes a validated, typed result to a database or state engine, and terminates its execution lifecycle. Agent B is then instantiated independently, pulling only the specific key fields required to execute its assigned role. This decoupled pattern enforces clean execution boundaries, prevents context contamination, and keeps token costs linear rather than exponential.

To build resilient multi-agent systems in production, enterprise architectures are pivoting away from unconstrained “agent chat” and toward structured operational protocols. Standardized specifications like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) demonstrate that real agent coordination relies on rigid schema boundaries, explicit tool capabilities, and controlled state persistence rather than free-form natural language handoffs. Similarly, emerging frameworks for cross-framework agent interoperability such as the open Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol focus on standardized discovery, capability negotiation, and secure payload routing rather than conversational mechanics.

Security and governance further demand that we abandon the conversational myth. Direct, unmonitored agent-to-agent exchanges create blind spots for prompt injection, indirect data poisoning, and unauthorized privilege escalation. If a malicious payload or unformatted data stream bypasses the input validation of an upstream agent, an unconstrained downstream agent will execute those malicious instructions without question. Enterprise-grade systems require every handoff to pass through deterministic guardrails: schema validation, authorization checks, and execution boundaries that treat every incoming agent payload with zero-trust skepticism.

Beyond security, observability becomes nearly impossible when agents communicate in unformatted chat streams. Engineering teams attempting to debug a failed workflow must sift through thousands of lines of conversational natural language to discover where an agent drifted off course. In contrast, when agent handoffs are structured as typed API calls or state transactions, every interaction generates deterministic logs, performance metrics, and explicit failure points that can be monitored, alerted on, and automatically retried using standard SRE tooling.

The path forward for multi-agent architecture is not teaching models how to hold better conversations with one another; it is designing superior deterministic state machines, memory stores, and interface boundaries. Until we stop framing multi-agent design around the metaphor of human conversation, teams will continue to drown in token costs and unpredictable runtime behavior. AI agents don’t need to talk; they need clean contracts, typed schemas, and reliable state routing.

Disclosure: All core technical concepts and conclusions are entirely my own. A GenAI tool was used strictly for prose refinement.

Abhilash Pakalapati is a Senior AI Engineer and Data Engineer with more than a decade of experience building large-scale data platforms and intelligent applications. His work focuses on the design of modern data architectures that support machine learning, generative AI systems, and real-time analytics in enterprise environments.

item.title: An Ethics Ecosystem for AI
item.dc:creator: John Basl
item.description: Making a case for the development of an AI ethics ecosystem.
item.content:encoded:
Attention to the social and ethical dimensions of AI has spurred efforts in industry, academia, and government to anticipate and mitigate ethical risks.9,29,38 Whether motivated by genuine moral concern or not, key stakeholders are increasingly dedicating significant resources to addressing ethical challenges in AI.a But despite these efforts, AI projects and products regularly cause controversy, and ethical missteps abound.

Key Insights

  • There are a variety of ethical failures in the research, development, and deployment of AI tools, but the purported solutions cannot address the scale of ethical challenges raised by AI across its application domains.

  • Other domains, including health and healthcare, manage widespread and varied ethical challenges through the use of ethics ecosystems, which organize collective work around a central set of values.

  • Taking an ecosystemic approach in AI reveals why alternatives that try to make use of tools from bioethics (and elsewhere) end up misapplying them, while also showing how to make progress in understanding the nature of AI ethical challenges and how to address them.

Frequently recommended responses to these ethical shortcomings include creating ethics tools and resources for specific sociotechnical contexts, upskilling in ethics for technologists and in technology for ethicists,12 and practicing participatory technology design that involves key stakeholders.6,8,36 These aims are laudable; however, they are inadequate for the scale and nature of the social and ethical challenges we face. We articulate an alternative response: We should work toward the development of an AI ethics ecosystem, an overlapping and mutually reinforcing network of governance, education, training, research, and communication mechanisms.

In what follows, we argue for the development of an AI ethics ecosystem (or collection of ecosystems) by first identifying a range of recurring ethical missteps and evaluating current attempts to address them. We then illustrate details of the ecosystemic approach, highlighting how ethics ecosystems in other domains or sectors—such as health and medicine, military and defense, and aviation—allow us to manage their particular social and moral challenges. Drawing especially on the ecosystem governing health research and practice, we identify the essential components of ethics ecosystems. We then argue that existing tools and practices in the AI domain fall well short of what would be required to realize an AI ethics ecosystem, and recommend concentrating our efforts on addressing that shortfall. In so doing, we reflect on lessons we can learn from difficulties faced in other domains, as well as on hurdles that may appear particular to the AI domain. The upshot of our reflection is not a detailed explanation of the specifics of a monolithic AI ethics ecosystem. Rather, it is a recognition that adopting the development of an AI ethics ecosystem as a goal changes our orientation to doing ethics work across sectors, domains, and populations, in a way that yields hope for addressing the diversity and scale of ethical challenges raised by AI and its integration across a broad range of sociotechnical systems.

Recurring Ethical Missteps

Among the kinds of ethical failures in AI is the misapplication of existing ethical tools. This occurs when we observe that some ethical challenge in the AI context closely resembles one from another context, and then too hastily import the tools of the latter in hopes of solving problems in the former. To illustrate, consider informed consent, a crucial ethical tool in the context of human subjects research (HSR) in the U.S. In that context, securing informed consent requires researchers to ensure participants are provided with clear information about how the research will be conducted and used, understand the associated risks, and are participating voluntarily. This operationalizes respect for autonomy and protects participants’ well-being. When this model is applied to the domain of AI or digital data collection, however, it is typically operationalized as “notice and choice,” which fails to serve those same values. In complex digital systems, true comprehension is rarely possible for end users: Information about data uses is often overly technical or incomplete, and the mechanisms for ensuring authentic understanding or voluntary participation, such as oversight by institutional review boards (IRBs), are not in place. As a result, the attempt to directly import the ethical tool from HSR to AI fails because it is not suited to safeguard foundational values in the new context.2

Ethical trouble also arises when we try to solve problems related to AI with insufficient technical understanding. This often occurs when ethicists, despite their normative expertise, build their analyses on incorrect assumptions about how the underlying technologies function, how they are engineered, or how they are deployed in the real world. To illustrate, consider the progression of the scholarly literature on autonomous vehicles (AVs) in philosophical ethics. As AV technology matured, philosophers recognized that self-driving cars presented new challenges with respect to the ethics of driving and related policy design. Early commentary in the field often treated some ethical challenges as real-world instantiations of the trolley problem, reasoning that the ethics of harm distribution from the thought experiment could be directly applied to driving scenarios that AVs might face on the road.21 But this way of thinking seems to rest on a misunderstanding about how complex robotic systems operate. The specific outcomes in any particular AV driving scenario are partly a function of how various machine learning systems in the vehicle are trained, and therefore a function of choices about how to construct their training regimes, including a multitude of choices about data collection, curation, validation, and so on. Questions about how best to construct and evaluate such regimes are themselves ethical questions with downstream implications across the range of scenarios in which AVs operate. Attempting to draw lessons directly from trolley cases about what we should design cars to do in discrete, superficially similar accident scenarios fundamentally misunderstands the nature of the technical design challenge at issue and how ethical tools can help us navigate that challenge.4

Unsurprisingly, a further kind of failure that regularly occurs mirrors the last: when sufficient technical understanding is met with insufficient ethical understanding. This is exemplified in much of the scholarship regarding fairness metrics in algorithmic decision making, especially in the earliest days of that literature. In response to troubling cases in which prediction or recommendation systems apparently treated subjects quite differently, and unfairly, depending on their membership in various protected classes, a lot of energy was devoted toward mathematically defining fairness conditions that could be used to constrain the modeling in systems of that kind, such that their outputs would be guaranteed to avoid the problems of the troubling cases.10 While understandable and even laudable, the difficulty with such efforts is there is no good reason to think that the whole of the ethical import of fairness can be captured by easily codifiable conditions such as formal fairness metrics,10 especially given that fairness is often a matter of attending to procedural details in decision making,13 or of ensuring that decisions go some way to addressing past or structural injustice, either in addition to or rather than outcomes. As the enormous body of scholarship on the normative significance of fairness evinces, there is little reason to expect that fairness is the kind of normative value that we care about in just the same way, for just the same reasons, across the wide range of contexts in which people are subject to algorithmic sorting or prediction. For example, consider how we might differentially evaluate whether a recidivism prediction tool is fair depending on whether it is used in pretrial detention decisions or to provide resources to communities or individuals to reduce the risk of reoffense. Whether failing to satisfy a given fairness metric is unfair depends on a variety of facts about the context-specific use of a given tool. It was a mistake at the outset, then, to understand the problematic cases that jump-started the literature as requiring a solution in the form of univocal, mathematically operationalized fairness standards.b

A final form of failure can occur when it seems like everything has gone right: We have identified some problem that can be addressed with AI, carefully considered the technical and ethical issues at play, and created a tool that looks promising. The problem? No one wants it. When potential users turn away from a promising computing solution, we believe that this is often due to failed stakeholder engagement. During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in the U.S. in 2020, digital tools were developed with the promise of efficiently notifying users of potential exposures. Among them was the Google/Apple Exposure Notification (GAEN) system, which had been designed with special attention to privacy protection. Digital tools were largely inefficacious in the U.S. due to low uptake, seemingly explained in large part by lack of trust.16 Despite the sophistication of its privacy-protecting methods, many Americans were reluctant to use GAEN for fear of privacy violations. Why? At least part of the answer is that they seemed to conflate the technology that enabled exposure notification with other forms of technology designed to enable contact tracing, and so took GAEN to be just as much of a privacy threat as, say, location tracking. That conflation reveals a failure of communication between those building and hoping to deploy the technology and those who might have benefited from it.

Lessons

The ethical failures above point to several natural interventions that might help address them.

One natural solution is to provide cross-disciplinary training. Indeed, educational interventions are regularly recommended by major institutional actors, and several such programs are already well developed and have been operating for several years.12,14,20 An alternative solution addresses the problem of misunderstanding across disciplinary lines differently, by fostering the development of teams of researchers comprising experts from different areas of study.28

The natural solution to failed stakeholder engagement in technology design is obvious: Increase the degree to which stakeholders are involved. A recent National Academies report endorses just that idea: “Projects that include among their aims the achievement of societally relevant outcomes should engage stakeholders from the start of design through deployment, testing, and redesign processes, and employ design teams that include domain experts and social and behavioral scientists to help ensure the project is solving the right problems.”12  The most well-known method by which to accomplish this kind of aim is participatory design, which the report approvingly cites just a few sentences later.

Each of these ideas gets something right, and we are enthusiastic about some particularly well-developed attempts to implement them. We are pessimistic, however, about their prospects for systematically resolving the pain points canvassed in the previous section. Despite the natural fit between the shape of the problems and solutions on offer, there is a vast mismatch between the size or scale of the problems and solutions. Consider, for example, what it would take to try to resolve the problems through “upskilling” technical and/or normative experts. Because of how pervasively AI is being implemented across the major sectors of society, it would be a monumental undertaking to ensure that all of the actors directly engaged in such projects had expert-level understanding of both the technological components of their work and the relevant ethical issues implicated by it. Concentrating instead on the composition of teams of researchers is unlikely to help. Given the many teams across industry, academic, and governmental settings conducting cutting-edge AI research, we doubt the existing supply of normative expertise would be close to matching the demand that would exist should each of them require a minimally tech-competent ethicist to join their ranks. The scaling difficulties for participatory design are perhaps even worse. Indeed, the challenges of scaling are such that attempts to overcome them may cut against the very theoretical underpinnings that motivate participatory design in the first place. And, again, the pervasiveness of AI research and implementation only exacerbates this problem.37,40

As we will see, the mismatch between the problems we face and an attempted resolution in the form of education and stakeholder engagement becomes clearer when we consider how we respond to pervasive ethical challenges in other domains.

An Ecosystemic Approach

Addressing the ethical challenges raised by AI is best accomplished through the cultivation of an ethics ecosystem, a collection of coordinated, mutually supporting components oriented toward preserving, protecting, and promoting the foundational values of some domain of activity. It is useful to think of the collection of components as an ecosystem insofar as it enables us to understand and assess how the components and their relationships to one another serve the overall function of realizing the values that they are designed to jointly promote and protect.c While details vary, more or less robust ecosystems serve this function across a variety of domains, including healthcare, engineering, the military, and law. The foundational values that ecosystems promote, preserve, and protect are typically developed into intermediary norms, which clarify how the foundational values are typically realized in the domain.d For example, in HSR, the foundational value of respect for persons is protected through prioritizing the autonomy of research participants.3 In the case of animal subjects research (ASR), the foundational value of animal welfare is cashed out in terms of a set of intermediary norms referred to as the “3Rs”: replacement (of animal subjects where possible), reduction (of the number of animal subjects where possible), and refinement (of interventions to reduce the harm caused to animal subjects).17 In some sub-domains of engineering, the value of well-being is realized through intermediary norms focused on safety, around which a system of regulations, audits, and trainings is organized.11

The components of an ethics ecosystem specify and reinforce intermediary norms as a mechanism to preserve, promote, and protect foundational values. In this section, we articulate six key components of a well-functioning ethics ecosystem: ethics infrastructure; governance; education, training, and outreach; foundational to translational research; shared conceptual resources; and interdisciplinary ethics experts. We define each component, providing examples from existing ecosystems, before explaining two features that are essential to a well-functioning ecosystem that are distinct from the individual components: coordination and enculturation. To illuminate the components and features of well-functioning ethics ecosystems, we will point to examples from outside the AI domain, focusing mostly on the sub-domains and accompanying ecosystems related to health research and practice, including HSR, ASR, clinical care, and embryonic stem-cell research. In focusing our attention in this way, we do not mean to suggest that the health sector is the only domain that realizes a well-functioning ethics ecosystem (consider, for example, legal, military, and engineering domains).e Nor do we mean to suggest that the implementation details of these ecosystems are likely to be easily ported to AI—indeed, we were at pains above to illustrate some reasons for thinking they will not be. Rather, our hope is to draw attention to the mature, interconnected functional form of these systems to highlight the general shape and scale of what we believe is necessary in the case of AI.f

Ethics infrastructure.  Ethics infrastructure refers to the tools, rules, and operationalizations that govern the practices of those working within an ethics ecosystem. It also includes local oversight of those tools, rules, and operationalizations. This infrastructure can come in many forms; much of it might be automated or involve simple procedures and principles that researchers or practitioners can be trained to follow as part of their daily practice. For example, it may include standard auditing procedures, mechanisms for stakeholders to easily escalate issues that require more careful attention or expertise that they lack, and other forms of direct guidance for actors enmeshed throughout the ecosystem.

That brief description might seem to imply a recommendation for a kind of compliance regime for managing ethical issues, one that reduces addressing complex ethical scenarios to a box-checking exercise. While we agree that mere legal compliance is often a bare-minimum requirement that is generally inadequate for addressing the ethical dimensions of technological practice, compliance need not mean mere legal compliance and box-checking need not be an exercise devoid of substantive ethical value. It is possible to develop operationalized ethics tools that go beyond legal requirements that researchers, practitioners, and other key stakeholders can be trained to use without requiring significant ethical competency themselves. These operationalizations can include escalation procedures that pull in those with such competency when necessary. When situated within a robust ethics ecosystem, the use of these operationalizations is part of a useful division of labor for the intricate work carried out by the whole.

As concrete examples of ethics infrastructure, consider the various tools and methods employed in the health sector. In research involving human participants in the U.S., researchers must make a determination of whether the research constitutes “human subjects research,” whether such research satisfies criteria for exemption, and, if so, whether that exemption means they need either no or an expedited research review from their IRB. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) offers a decision tool for making these determinations, requiring researchers to make use of it in the course of securing approval to conduct human subjects research.32 Researchers provide a relatively standardized set of documents that include a research protocol describing their proposed study and how participants will be recruited, the information that they will disclose to research participants and how that information will be disclosed, information about the study population and whether participants are members of vulnerable populations, and documentation confirming that researchers have completed various mandatory trainings. These documents are ultimately submitted to an IRB, the local oversight mechanism, which reviews them with an eye toward ensuring, for example, that duties to disclose, inform, and avoid coercion are satisfied and that there is sufficient justification for using participants from vulnerable populations. There are also standard sets of principles that researchers can utilize when seeking ethical guidance concerning their research, such as the NIH Guiding Principles for Ethical Research.26 In the U.S., similar procedures guide ASR, with appropriate documentation being submitted for review by an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC).39

Local oversight mechanisms are a key part of the ethics infrastructure of an ethics ecosystem and also involve operationalizations and mechanisms that help realize the ethical aims of the ecosystem. IRBs and IACUCs have standard monitoring procedures for the studies they approve.33 For example, IACUCs organize periodic site visits to animal labs to monitor the treatment of animals. The oversight boards also have composition requirements that help ensure the relevant expertise is present on the board to carry out effective oversight and avoid conflicts of interest: IACUCs must have a veterinarian as a member, and both IRBs and IACUCs require scientific and non-scientific members as well as non-affiliated or external members.30,39,g

Governance.  Robust ethics ecosystems are governed by a broad system of rules, norms, rewards, and formal and informal accountability mechanisms, including sanctions that incentivize and support other components of the ecosystem. For example, this system might incentivize, perhaps very strongly, the adoption of particular pieces of ethics infrastructure or various education and training requirements. The governance component of an ethics ecosystem sits outside any single institution or organization, creating mechanisms that make those individual organizations and institutions responsive to broader social concerns. Laws, regulation, and legislation are obvious pieces of this component of the ecosystem, but they are not the only form. Broadly shared social norms, for example, can provide the kinds of incentives to deploy ethics infrastructure, engage in training, fund domain-relevant ethics research, and so on. Accreditation requirements for educational institutions are another mechanism by which some form of ecosystemic governance can be enacted.h

In the cases of human and animal subjects research, the policy, regulation, and accountability frameworks are largely enshrined in the law. An example is the “Common Rule” governing HSR, which includes requirements on institutions to ensure compliance with a set of rules and regulations, on researchers with respect to how they manage issues of informed consent, and on the workings (constitution, function, etc.) of IRBs.31 Similarly, the Animal Welfare Act enacts analogous requirements governing ASR and its local oversight.39 While typical (and useful), governance and oversight need not be mandated by law.i

Education, training, and outreach.  Healthy ethics ecosystems include mechanisms to educate and train participants, as well as to engage key stakeholders through targeted outreach. These efforts aim to promote a shared understanding of the structures and processes that uphold and protect the foundational values of the ecosystem. This component facilitates the onboarding of practitioners, equipping them to navigate the ethics ecosystem effectively and to apply its ethical principles and tools in their own work.

In health and scientific research contexts, education and training requirements are established by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF).27 These requirements include responsible conduct of research (RCR) training, as well as specific instruction in HSR and ASR. RCR, HSR, and ASR training are integrated into undergraduate curricula, and additional ethics training is often mandated in graduate programs. Members of IRBs and IACUCs are subject to further specialized training. Much of this educational infrastructure is maintained by the Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative (CITI), which delivers and certifies foundational ethics training in both human and animal subjects research.7

Outreach is perhaps the least developed component of existing ethics ecosystems. Nevertheless, some important cornerstones are well-established and newer efforts are underway to enhance engagement with key stakeholders. For example, in 1990, the NIH established the Ethics, Legal, and Social Implications (ELSI) Research Program to examine these dimensions of genetics and genomics research.24 Much of ELSI research focuses on engaging stakeholders—including patients and the broader public—to understand their values and perspectives on genetic research. There is also a growing emphasis on partnering with communities through community advisory boards (CABs), which serve as mechanisms for integrating stakeholder values and fostering community collaboration in research.35 The importance of transparent and effective science communication with the public is widely recognized, and the NIH maintains a standardized checklist to guide communication about health and clinical research.25,j

Foundational to translational research.  No matter how robust the other key components of an ethics ecosystem at any given moment, we should expect that some ethical issues will remain unresolved and that novel concerns will emerge. Sociotechnical domains are in this way dynamic: They evolve and we come to recognize new ethical dimensions of that evolution, or a newly recognized ethical failing of the past helps us to recognize a previously unidentified vulnerability in the ecosystem. A well-functioning ethics ecosystem requires an ethics research component to help identify, understand, and resolve ongoing and emerging ethical challenges. The ethics research component will itself have a number of sub-components that help resolve foundational ethics challenges and then translate that throughout the ecosystem, leading to updates in ethics infrastructure, education, governance, and so on.

In the context of health, the field of bioethics includes the key components of foundational to translational research. Bioethics is a robust field with scholars and practitioners conducting research on the full-range of ethical issues related to health, healthcare, and medical practice. Research spans foundational issues—for example, on the ultimate normative foundations of research ethics and how that should push us to revise our ethics infrastructure—and applied issues—for example, empirical work on the effectiveness of various consent procedures. There are high-impact journals, such as Bioethics, and conferences for dissemination and information exchange. There are also case libraries and gatherings of IRBs and IACUCs to share information and approaches to managing particular complications.34 There is significant bioethics research funding to sustain this work, often tied to more general research funding in the health sector.

Shared conceptual resources.  Two core components of an ethics ecosystem support and enable the ecosystem more broadly. The first is a shared conceptual and linguistic landscape: a relatively broad, shared understanding of key concepts and terminology that facilitates communication and action across the ethics ecosystem.

We have already referenced various bits of the shared conceptual and linguistic landscape in the U.S.-based context.k For example, within HSR, informed consent is a term of art, picking out a variety of specific requirements or duties (disclosure, informedness, and non-coercion) and carrying significant weight. Those regularly engaged with the HSR ethics ecosystem know that “exempt” research has a specific meaning (and that, confusingly to outsiders, it does not mean that the research is exempt from IRB review). Within the ASR ecosystem, one can casually mention the 3Rs and expect that those listening will understand.

Interdisciplinary ethics experts.  The second core enabling component of a healthy ethics ecosystem is the presence of interdisciplinary ethics scholars and practitioners who execute and facilitate various ecosystemic functions. Interdisciplinary experts help carry out oversight, conduct ethics research and translate it into practice, and inform regulation, and are trained to command a much broader understanding of the ecosystem as a whole than others working more locally within it.

In the health space, this component is, again, very robust. The education component of the ecosystem includes pathways for training bioethicists. Bioethicists carry out significant research agendas and play a significant role in oversight, governance, education, and training; they deploy (and advance) the conceptual and linguistic landscape to facilitate interactions between the components.

Features of an ethics ecosystem: Coordination and enculturation.  Before turning to our assessment of the current state of the ethics ecosystem for AI and big data, it is worth highlighting two additional features of a robust, well-functioning ethics ecosystem that are not themselves independent components but nonetheless make for a healthy ethics ecosystem: coordination and enculturation.

An ethics ecosystem is coordinated to the extent that there are reinforcing interactions between particular components. For example, in a well-functioning ecosystem, the education component prepares future practitioners to deploy the ethics infrastructure they will need to make use of. The governance component incentivizes those education requirements and sanctions violations of the ethics infrastructure. Research journals in the field will promote scholarship that is responsive to the relevant empirical facts about the ethics ecosystem as it is currently instantiated, and so on.

It should be apparent from our earlier discussions of the various ethics ecosystems in health that they are relatively well-coordinated. The descriptions of various components make reference to others. The Common Rule has specific implications for local oversight and other pieces of ethics infrastructure, as does the Animal Welfare Act. Ethics education in the health curriculum familiarizes students with key terminology and concepts, and there are distinct educational pathways to train bioethicists that then support other ecosystemic functions.

Robust ethics ecosystems possess another feature that augments their efficacy: enculturation. By this we mean that people within the ecosystem come to view their work through the lens of its values and processes. Someone who has been enculturated into an ethics ecosystem will start to parse ethical problems using the concepts and language of that ecosystem. This enculturation can be an effective mechanism for carrying out ecosystemic functions. For example, enculturation might facilitate effective use of the ethics infrastructure by reinforcing the attitude that the use of that infrastructure is part of what it is to be a good member of the community.

Extant ethics ecosystems that are relatively well-functioning exhibit this feature. In our many combined years of experience discussing ethics with people across a variety of domains, those conversations with people working in the health sector have a very different character from those with people in the military or defense domain, and differ again from discussions with those in cybersecurity, or civil engineering, or the law. While ethical reasoning within any of these domains is not a monolith and individuals differ in their attitudes regarding the ethical defaults and framings in the domain, our experience suggests widely shared intra-domain approaches to how people think about ethics. We surmise that this enculturation explains why, for example, much of the discussion of AI ethics issues in the domain of warfare has focused on responsibility and the importance of having a human in the loop, while discussions of AI in health and healthcare are frequently oriented around issues of data privacy and consent.

Conclusion: Ethics Ecosystems and AI

We expect that many readers will recognize the ways in which the current state of the ethics ecosystem for AI, to the extent that one exists at all, is deficient across the components and features we have discussed. To be sure, there is much work that falls under the heading of one or the other of the components outlined above: There is work on creating ethics infrastructure, developing governance, providing ethics education, and so on. However, most of these components are not mature and do not adequately serve their ecosystemic function. For example, while the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework (RMF) correctly identifies some foundational values in the domain and is sensitive to the need to operationalize them across differing applications, it takes significant work to move from the AI RMF to the kind of ethics infrastructure that could be widely deployed to researchers and practitioners across the domain.38 Even setting aside these difficulties, there are very few formal or informal accountability mechanisms or incentive architectures to orient stakeholders to adopt or closely follow whatever ethics infrastructure is available, and there are currently few developed mechanisms such as licensure that can be leveraged to develop those accountability mechanisms. Furthermore, the components as developed hardly stand in the sort of coordinated, mutually supporting relationships that would constitute an ethics ecosystem. For example, efforts to embed ethics modules within computer science curricula include no explicit attempts to align their work with the NIST AI RMF, and there exists no party whose role it is to enact such alignment.

We recognize that the call for a robust, coordinated ethics ecosystem to govern AI and big data is ambitious and may be met with skepticism for a number of reasons, including that the extant ethics ecosystems we identify as exemplars are themselves imperfect. While we cannot canvass and respond to all the grounds for skepticism here, we think it is important to highlight some lessons we can draw from current ecosystems. First, these ecosystems are relatively effective and efficient at managing a wide range of domain-specific ethical challenges, even when they might be inadequate with respect to others. Even recognizing that an ethics ecosystem for AI might not be perfect, an ecosystemic approach offers us perhaps the best opportunity to address the scale of the ethical challenge we face. Second, some of our most robust ethics ecosystems and the mechanisms that enable them are relatively young: The Belmont Report, the foundation of contemporary HSR protections in the U.S., was published in 1979, less than 50 years ago. This should give us hope that the development of the relevant components of ethics ecosystems need not be a dream for a distant future. Third, the strongest critiques of ethics ecosystems are themselves a product of these ecosystems: It is bioethicists trained within their ecosystem raising the most pressing criticisms of it. The lesson is that a robust ethics ecosystem for AI provides the resources to build ethical capacity that is oriented toward improving the ecosystem itself. Fourth, despite the above considerations, extant ethics ecosystems can become entrenched and difficult to change. While bioethicists have raised excellent critiques of the bioethics ecosystem, large-scale change has been slow and the ecosystem is still reasonably seen as deficient in a number of ways. Rather than seeing this as a reason to avoid implementing ethics ecosystems in other domains, we take this observation as informing the best way to cultivate and maintain an AI ethics ecosystem, by instituting practices designed to foster critical reflection and allow for nimble adjustment as needed. It also motivates the call for AI-specific ethics ecosystems, as opposed to simply modifying existing ethics ecosystems to accommodate AI. These ecosystems are largely entrenched, and were built prior to the development of AI. They are thereby oriented toward different individuals and professions, different sociotechnical features, and so on. The creation of an AI ethics ecosystem provides fertile ground for managing the intersection of AI and other domains.

Despite the ambitiousness of the call to adopt an ecosystemic approach, we feel that such an approach, sensitive to the successes and pitfalls of existing ecosystems, provides the best opportunity for addressing the scale and diversity of challenges raised by AI. The precise form of the individual components of such an ecosystem or collection of ecosystems is left open by what we have said, as is the issue of the number of sub-ecosystems that would best serve the domain. And, harkening back to an earlier lesson, we will not be able to simply adopt an existing ethics ecosystem. However, conceptualizing the ethical challenge for AI as one of developing an ethics ecosystem should itself influence how we assess our options for moving forward and shape calls to action for the discipline of computer science. Taking an ecosystemic approach should significantly reorient our thinking about a range of ethics interventions, from developing approaches to managing individual projects;22 to how we think about large-scale interventions in education, policy, and with the public; to how we think about the relationship among all of these. A careful, coordinated, holistic project of building and maintaining a healthy AI ethics ecosystem is our best hope for protecting ourselves from the ethical pitfalls of AI and developing AI technology that promotes human flourishing.
