item.title: GenAI Is Shipping Code Faster Than You Can Read It
item.dc:creator: Rahul Vaish
item.description: The silent question many coders are asking is if they can follow all of the code, or are perhaps falling behind.
item.content:encoded:
Open your team’s board on a Monday morning and the picture has already changed. Tickets that were open on Friday are closed. Pull requests that didn’t exist an hour ago are merged. A teammate shipped a feature over the weekend that, a year ago, would have taken a sprint. Much of the code was drafted by an AI assistant, reviewed quickly, and is already running in production.

If you feel a small knot of anxiety reading that, you’re in good company. Developers have always had to keep up with new frameworks and tools. What’s different now is how fast the code changes inside the codebase you’re responsible for. Code is arriving faster than anyone can read it, and the silent question many of us carry is: if I can’t follow all of this, am I falling behind? This post offers practical ways to work with the pace instead of being worn down by it.

The New Shape of FOMO

The classic fear of missing out (FOMO) in tech was about technologies: the language you hadn’t learned, the framework everyone else seemed to be using. The AI-era version is different. It’s about comprehension. You’re not worried about missing a tool; you’re worried about no longer understanding your own system.

That’s a more uncomfortable feeling, because it touches professional identity. Developers have traditionally earned trust by knowing how things work. When a large share of the change in a repository is machine-drafted and merged within hours, that sense of mastery can feel as if it’s slipping, even when your own output is higher than ever.

Why the Comparison is Broken

Much of the anxiety comes from measuring yourself against a dashboard. Merged pull requests, closed tickets, and lines changed are easy to count, so they are what we notice. But they only tell you how much was produced. They don’t tell you whether the change was architecturally correct, whether anyone else understands it well enough to build on top of it, or whether it will still make sense to the team in six months.

Think of a newsroom where the reporters suddenly start writing ten times faster. The editors still read at the same speed, so stories pile up waiting to be checked, and the editor’s attention becomes the limit. Software is the same. AI can write code quickly, but people still have to read it, understand it, and answer for it at human speed.

So the developer who tries to read every change isn’t the most diligent person on the team. They’re spending their scarcest resource, attention, on every change equally, including the ones that don’t need it. What matters now is knowing which changes deserve your attention, and that’s a skill you can build.

Practical Ways to Cope

None of these strategies ask you to read more. They’re about deciding where your attention goes.

● Start with one part and go deep: You’re accountable for the whole system, but you can’t know all of it at once, so don’t try. Start with the one part that matters most, maybe the one that paged someone last quarter or the one every feature seems to touch, and learn it properly. When it feels familiar, add the next. Keep only a rough outline of the rest. Depth grows one part at a time, and the anxiety shrinks with it.

● Let a weekly briefing do the streaming: Think of the morning digest an editor reads before deciding which stories need a closer look. Ask your team’s approved AI tool to read last week’s merged changes and write you one: a few plain-language bullet points on what changed, plus a sequence diagram of one or two key flows, like placing an order or logging in, showing what calls what and where it can fail. Try it by hand once to see if it’s useful, then put it on a weekly schedule so it doesn’t depend on anyone remembering. Read it over a coffee and you’ll spot things like a new fraud check before payment or a retry that was quietly introduced, even in parts of the system you don’t know well.

● Read what gets flagged like an editor: When the briefing flags a change, or a change lands in the part you know deeply, slow down. Ask whether the design fits the system, what the generated code quietly assumes, and what happens when it fails. Everything else gets a skim, and that’s fine. As generating code gets cheaper, the person who can quickly judge whether a change is sound becomes the most valuable one in the room. Review isn’t a tax on productivity anymore; it’s the craft.

● Follow one thread a week: Pick one item from the briefing, or one flow you’ve never traced, and follow it all the way down. Read the module you didn’t write, or work through the design behind it. An hour is usually enough. Depth builds on itself in a way scanning never does, and it’s the best cure for the feeling of skating on the surface.

● Say it out loud: This feeling is far more common than people admit. Mention it in a retro or a one-on-one and you’ll likely find others feel it too, and the weekly briefing is an easy thing to bring along. That’s usually where the conversation about smaller pull requests and better review habits starts.

What Teams and Leaders Can Do

A team that produces more than it can understand has a systems problem, so it needs systems answers, not just individual coping.

● Keep changes small enough to review. Smaller pull requests with a clear note on intent make review realistic, whether a person or a model wrote the code.

● Measure outcomes, not volume. Reliability, customer impact and time to recover say far more than merge counts, and they take away the pressure to compete on throughput.

● Budget time for understanding. Leave room for design reviews, documentation, and knowledge sharing. They’re what keeps a fast-moving codebase something people can still reason about.

A Steadier Way Forward

The speed of AI-assisted development is real and, for most teams, valuable. But it doesn’t change what makes an engineer worth trusting: sound judgment, a clear understanding of the systems they’re responsible for, and the discipline to focus on what matters. Those qualities aren’t made obsolete by a faster stream of code. They’re what make the stream safe to build on.

You don’t need to keep up with everything. You need to know what you’re accountable for, decide where your attention goes, and keep building the skills that machines make more important rather than less. The developers who thrive in this period won’t be the ones who read the most pull requests. They’ll be the ones who stay calm enough to ask the right questions: what changed, what could break, and what needs a closer look.

Rahul Vaish is a Software Engineer and Independent Researcher with over a decade of experience designing and building enterprise systems. His work focuses on software architecture, distributed systems, and applied AI.

item.title: AI Shakes Volunteer Sites
item.dc:creator: Samuel Greengard
item.description: The impact of AI on volunteer sites, including fake and misleading contributions and increasingly fewer queries, is creating unease about the future of sharing knowledge online.
item.content:encoded:
The generosity of strangers has long powered online communities. Spaces like Stack Overflow, GitHub, curl, OpenSSL, Wikipedia, and OpenStreetMap have a rich history of volunteers sharing knowledge and maintaining code, encyclopedias, and maps.

Now, AI is having a say. Trained on content from these sites, it is changing how volunteers contribute and how users consume content. Stack Overflow, for example, has seen monthly questions fall from a peak of roughly 200,000 in 2014 to about 1,400 in July 2026. Meanwhile, a deluge of contributions—often fake and misleading—has overrun these projects.

This has created unease about the future of online knowledge sharing. “We are starting to replace social communities and their underlying processes with a piece of software,” said Gordon Burtch, Allen and Kelli Questrom Professor in Information Systems at Boston University. “As fewer people go to the community with questions, the incentive for experts to be there falls in turn.”

He isn’t the only one sounding alarms. “There is a huge fear, with growing evidence, that AI companies are kicking the legs out from underneath the table they are eating at,” said Benjamin Mako Hill, an associate professor of communication at the University of Washington and a longtime contributor to peer-production projects.

The stakes extend beyond site traffic and human connections. Fundamental questions arise about the quality of AI-provided information, who owns and profits from it, and what role humans play in vetting it. The cycle can also be recursive: models trained on public knowledge inhibit the production of new content. The question now is: will these communities evolve or disappear?

Substance or Slop?

Every era has seen online communities wither or die. Usenet groups, mailing lists, and the discussion boards on CompuServe and AOL, evolved into more elaborate Web forums. Those resources eventually turned into Stack Overflow, GitHub, and Reddit. At each transition, participants lamented but the world moved on.

Whether AI will supplant human contributors or introduce new forms of knowledge sharing is not clear. What is apparent is that peer production projects are undergoing a radical shift—and the repercussions could be far reaching. “AI creates an asymmetry of sorts. Generation becomes costless, but verification, evaluation, and curation do not,” Burtch said.

At curl, tldraw, and English-language Wikipedia, AI has lowered production costs and increased participation—but with few checks on verification, judgment, and context. Curl’s seven-year bug bounty ended in January 2026 after roughly a fifth of submissions were deemed AI slop, and fewer than 5% turned out to be actual vulnerabilities. Over its lifetime, the program paid researchers more than $100,000 for identifying 87 confirmed vulnerabilities.

AI also can reduce participation. Disintermediation on the Internet has existed for well over a decade. Google knowledge panels have pulled content from Wikipedia and other services. The problem, Hill argues, is that corrections and nuance don’t travel back to the original source. When a user challenges a chatbot’s answer, that suggestion remains in the chat window. And unlike a search result, the chatbot doesn’t always reveal where the information originated.

At Stack Overflow, site rules compound the problem. A question that has already been answered is typically marked “closed” and linked to the earlier thread. No new discussion takes place. This may not seem significant since past content remains, but “if new people don’t join and participate, there is nobody there to grow into a community leader or moderator,” Burtch said. “The community is likely to atrophy and become more concentrated. It may take longer, or become impossible, to cover new technologies.”

There is evidence this is taking place. Stack Overflow was already in slow decline prior to AI, said Johannes Wachs, an associate professor at Hungary’s Corvinus University of Budapest and a senior fellow at Microsoft’s AI Economy Institute. Once ChatGPT appeared, one study found activity dropped by 25% within six months relative to comparable forums where the chatbot was less available or less capable. By Wachs’s account, overall use of Stack Overflow has fallen more than 95% since ChatGPT’s release. “Online communities thrive on new blood,” he said.

Labor Pains

The irony is inescapable: AI models are built on the backs of the same communities they are displacing. Stack Overflow answers, Wikipedia articles, and millions of GitHub commits became training data, yet the volunteers who generated them were neither asked nor paid. When Stack Overflow entered a licensing agreement with OpenAI in 2024, the contributors didn’t receive a penny from the deal, and they had no say in how their content is used.

“It’s essentially a question of who owns the platform to distribute content, and who owns the right to the content,” said Hanlin Li, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin. Currently, she said, platforms can distribute or resell what volunteers produce however they like, and “the actual creators don’t often see any benefits from that distribution.”

That rift was exposed in 2023, when Stack Exchange moderators went on strike for nearly two months after the company issued confusing instructions about its AI policy. Days into the walkout, it also stopped publishing its data dumps to the Internet Archive while making plans to monetize its API for data access. For communities that had long embraced the principle of open knowledge, the shift in policy was devastating. It laid bare the gulf between producing knowledge and controlling how it is used and monetized.

Li believes volunteers have leverage because, as new events unfold and new information emerges, AI models require a steady supply of fresh data from humans. She points to Wikipedia as a success story. The English-language site actively deletes AI-generated content. In addition, rather than blocking reuse, the Wikimedia Foundation has established a paid tier that sells high-volume customers a real-time feed of edits and article updates along with guaranteed uptime. It requires attribution and prohibits using the feed to build a competing product.

Beyond the Stars

Although the future of many online communities is cloudy, some—Reddit and GitHub among them—continue to thrive. The difference likely isn’t AI; it’s that some sites dispense answers and others offer a place to debate a topic or discuss a bug report. “The social fabric of Reddit is a real thing,” Wachs said. GitHub, likewise, isn’t a reference library but a place to work. Although much of the code arriving there is now written by AI, humans still decide what gets built and what gets merged.

Other sites, such as Stack Overflow, may already be in a death spiral. Yet the ending isn’t written. “We need to find a way for AI to complement the human knowledge-production process rather than disintermediate it,” Burtch said. “AI products should provide attribution and, where appropriate, return traffic, feedback, or financial support to the communities whose knowledge they use,” he added.

Wachs strikes a broader view: “There is a joy to participating in online communities. There is a reason people answer other people’s questions for no pay, and that’s the one thing that no model can provide.”

Samuel Greengard is an author and journalist based in West Linn, OR, USA.

item.title: Who Audits the AI Auditors?
item.dc:creator: Srinivas Padmanabhuni
item.description: Human judgment is still the strongest tool we have to address ambiguity, accountability, and genuine edge cases.
item.content:encoded:
I work as an AI assurance specialist at AiEnsured in Bengaluru. My job, in plain terms, is testing other people’s AI. That kind of work used to be optional hygiene. It is steadily becoming an operational requirement: regulators, banks, and large enterprises increasingly want independent verification before a probabilistic system goes anywhere near production.

That is progress. It is also a new risk, and one the industry talks about far less than it should.

The organizations that vouch for other people’s AI now sit on sensitive models, proprietary data and, increasingly, their own AI tooling. Which raises an obvious question that almost nobody in the room wants to answer out loud: who audits the AI auditors?

A Familiar Pattern, Three Familiar Gaps

Computing professionals know this pattern from software quality. Nobody accepts a vendor’s own unit tests as sufficient assurance for a flight-control system. We ask who tested it, against which oracle, with what independence, and what residual risk remains. AI assurance is catching up to that discipline, but unevenly. Three gaps appear again and again in practice.

Independence is assumed, not designed. An internal model-risk team, a consulting slide deck, and an external technical assessor are not interchangeable. Each can be useful. Only some of them can speak freely when the finding is inconvenient. Procurement language still rarely defines what “independent” means for AI testing: contractual freedom to deliver unvarnished findings, separation from the teams that built the model, and clear rules for handling residual risk.

Evidence is thinner than policy. Most enterprises now have AI principles, ethics boards, and acceptable-use documents. Far fewer can show repeatable tests with thresholds, named owners, and continuous monitoring. A fairness metric with no owner and no review cadence is theatre. So is a jailbreak demo that never becomes a regression suite. Assurance that cannot be replayed is very hard to audit.

The auditors use AI, too. Test-case generators, summarizers, and triage assistants bring their own failure modes: client context leaking into external models, overconfident summaries of vulnerability logs, silent drift in the helper model. If an assurance firm cannot inventory and govern its own AI use, buyers should treat that as a material risk, not a footnote.

What the Frameworks Do, and Do Not Do

The regulatory picture is real but partial. The EU AI Act imposes strict independence rules on notified bodies, the third parties that run conformity assessments for certain high-risk systems. Article 31 requires those bodies to be independent of the provider of the system under assessment, of any operator with an economic interest in it, and of the provider’s competitors. Neither the body, its top management, nor the personnel performing the assessment may be involved in the design, development, marketing, or use of the systems they assess, and consultancy work that could compromise independence of judgment is expressly barred. Impartiality procedures and liability insurance are mandatory. That is a serious answer, on paper.

The catch is coverage. For most high-risk uses listed in Annex III, Article 43 routes providers through the internal-control procedure of Annex VI, which means self-assessment with no notified body involved. Third-party assessment is concentrated in narrower cases, mainly certain biometric systems when harmonized standards are not fully applied. The Act hard-codes independence where external assessment is mandatory, and leaves a large share of high-risk systems to the provider’s own processes.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework takes the opposite approach: voluntary, process-oriented. Its Measure function recommends involving independent assessors, or internal experts who were not front-line developers, specifically to reduce bias and conflicts of interest. It prescribes no certified auditor class. It treats independent review as a way to strengthen measurement inside an organization’s own risk process, which is useful, and easy to skip.

The standards community is filling part of the gap. ISO/IEC 42001:2023, described by ISO as the world’s first AI management system standard, forces evidence of accountability rather than one-off technical claims: who owns AI risk, how risks are assessed and treated, how changes are controlled, how incidents are learned from. India has adopted it nationally through the Bureau of Indian Standards. Just as relevant to my title question, ISO/IEC 42006:2025 sets requirements for the bodies that audit and certify organizations against ISO/IEC 42001, supplementing the general auditing rules of ISO/IEC 17021-1 with AI-specific expectations on competence, impartiality, and consistency. It defines what the certifier must demonstrate before its stamp means anything. ISO/IEC 23894 adds guidance on AI risk management across the lifecycle. None of this is sufficient on its own, but the shape of an answer is emerging.

Professional and standards bodies have moved in the same direction. IEEE’s 7000-series standards address ethical concerns, transparency, and algorithmic bias in system design. ACM’s Code of Ethics asks computing professionals for comprehensive and thorough evaluation of systems and their impacts, and ACM policy statements call for auditability and independent scrutiny of algorithmic systems. Yet none of these frameworks, on its own or together, establishes one universal regime for overseeing the auditors of everyday AI systems.

The Human Bottleneck

Human judgment is still the strongest tool we have to address ambiguity, accountability, and genuine edge cases. People weigh context that is not in the training data, spot the statistically plausible output that is still unacceptable, and can stand behind a decision when a regulator asks who signed off. An AI system cannot be held responsible in the ordinary sense. Someone has to be.

But judgment does not scale. Ask a person to approve every output or every action, and fatigue and automation bias arrive quickly. People over-trust confident recommendations, click through repetitive prompts, and miss the rare serious error precisely when the system is mostly right. In agentic settings the problem is sharper: an agent can initiate hundreds of actions, and per-action human approval becomes rubber-stamping or simple operational impossibility. Scaling judgment is a design problem, not a staffing slogan. It needs risk-tiered oversight, human-on-the-loop monitoring with selective intervention, clear escalation thresholds, and measurement of the review process itself.

What the Community Should Demand

So what should we, as computing professionals, actually ask for?

Ask assurance providers for the same class of proof we demand of AI vendors. Not a product pitch: evidence. The scope of the assessment, the methods and benchmarks used, the known limitations, the data-handling controls, and how the firm governs AI inside its own delivery. Prefer providers who can show a managed system for AI risk, not only a toolkit. Treat standards such as ISO/IEC 42001, and the competence and impartiality rules of ISO/IEC 42006 for the certifiers themselves, as necessary but not sufficient. They organize accountability. They do not replace technical tests for bias, robustness, security, or drift.

For researchers and tool builders, the opportunity is to make assurance itself measurable: shared benchmarks for LLM application testing, clearer reporting formats for fairness and robustness findings, and evaluation methods that survive model updates. For educators, AI quality belongs next to software engineering and security in the curriculum. The next generation of engineers will ship probabilistic systems. They also will be asked to vouch for them.

I am not arguing that every tester must hold the same certificate, or that management-system audits replace hands-on evaluation. I am arguing for symmetry. As AI assurance moves from optional hygiene to regulatory and contractual necessity, the people who test AI should expect to be tested on how they run their own house.

Trust in AI will not come from louder assurances. It will come from evidence that travels, including evidence about the auditors.

Srinivas Padmanabhuni is CTO and co-founder of testAIng.com/AiEnsured, where he works as an AI assurance specialist. He is a member of an expert group contributing to draft AI regulation in India, a member of a TMMi AI testing expert committee, and co-author of one of the first AI testing certification syllabi, which fed into ISTQB’s Certified Tester AI Testing. He works on AI quality, software engineering, and responsible AI.

item.title: Escaping the Cloud with Edge RAG
item.dc:creator: Muralikrishna Veeramosu
item.description: Relying on infinite cloud context windows is an unsustainable economic and architectural model. The solution is to abandon the cloud altogether for sensitive financial reasoning.
item.content:encoded:
In my experience architecting AI systems for heavily regulated environments, I have encountered a profound privacy-utility paradox that currently is paralyzing the integration of generative AI in consumer finance.

On the one hand, users demand the hyper-personalized, autonomous wealth management capabilities promised by modern AI. They want to open their mobile banking app and ask deeply contextual, cross-account questions, like:

● “Why did my discretionary spending spike last month?”
● “Can you cross-reference my checking account and my Amex statement to see if I was double-charged for the hotel stay in Paris?”
● “If I divert $500 a month from my tech-stock ETF to a high-yield savings account, how will that impact my goal of buying a house in two years?”

On the other hand, transmitting years of highly sensitive, personally identifiable financial data to a centralized, third-party cloud large language model (LLM) to answer these questions creates unacceptable regulatory and cybersecurity liabilities. Under frameworks like GDPR, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, and the emerging Digital Operational Resilience Act, moving user ledgers across network boundaries to a black-box cloud API is a massive structural risk.

For the past few years, the enterprise has tried to build secure vaults using inherently porous cloud architectures. We have relied on complex data anonymization techniques, strict enterprise API agreements, and transient cloud instances. But these are bandages. As I have argued previously regarding the enterprise Token Trap, relying on infinite cloud context windows is an unsustainable economic and architectural model.1

The ultimate solution is not to build a more secure cloud pipeline; the solution is to abandon the cloud altogether for sensitive financial reasoning.

The Era of the Sovereign Financial Agent

We are entering the era of the sovereign financial agent. The core philosophy of this architecture is an inversion of standard cloud computing: we must bring the intelligence to the data, rather than sending the data to the intelligence.

Historically, this was impossible due to the sheer computational weight of language models. However, with the advent of the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) and the unified memory architecture in modern iPhones, mobile edge computing has reached a critical inflection point. Unlike traditional systems that partition memory between the CPU and GPU—requiring data to be inefficiently copied back and forth—Apple’s unified memory allows both processors to access the exact same data pool instantly.

Combined with Apple’s release of the MLX framework—an open-source machine learning framework designed specifically to exploit this Apple silicon architecture2—developers now can run quantized small language models locally with unprecedented speed and efficiency. By leveraging MLX Swift, a highly capable reasoning engine can be pushed directly into the user’s pocket.

However, deploying a raw model locally is only half the battle. To act as a financial advisor, the model must be context-aware.

The On-Device RAG Architecture

To give the on-device model context without pinging a cloud database, the mobile application must execute a localized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Edge RAG) pipeline entirely offline.

In a traditional cloud-based RAG setup, a software architect relies on heavy, deep-learning transformer models (like BERT) to generate text embeddings, which are then stored in a massive, centralized vector database. If you attempt to replicate this naive architecture on a smartphone—trying to load a 3GB embedding model simultaneously alongside a 3GB language model—the application will instantly crash.

To build Edge RAG on iOS, the architecture must be carefully decoupled to minimize RAM load:

  1. Native Embeddings Over Heavy Transformers: Instead of loading a secondary transformer model for vectorization, developers can utilize Apple’s built-in NLEmbedding class via the native Natural Language framework.3 This tool generates text vectors and calculates similarity rankings locally with sub-15-millisecond latency by taking advantage of CPU SIMD vector primitives directly on the Neural Engine.
  2. Local Vector Storage: Chunks of the user’s financial ledger, recent transaction history, and parsed PDF statements are vectorized and stored in a lightweight local framework running entirely within the iOS application sandbox (such as SQLite or SwiftData).
  3. Streamed Inference: When a user asks a complex financial question, the system performs a local cosine similarity search against the SQLite database, retrieves the top relevant financial context,

The result is an AI that “reads” your financial history and answers your questions without a single byte of personal data ever leaving the smartphone.

Navigating the Memory Wall: A18 vs. A19 Pro Architectures

While the hardware capabilities of modern smartphones are remarkable, building autonomous agents on mobile edge devices requires rigorous engineering discipline. As I recently observed when evaluating clinical AI deployments, relying on pristine cloud models is an illusion when edge reality demands highly constrained, small-data architectures.4 The boundaries of this architecture are dictated directly by the hardware generation the user holds.

On baseline and older architectures (such as the Apple A18 Pro and the base A19 chip), devices are equipped with 8GB of LPDDR5X RAM. However, the iOS kernel enforces a strict, unforgiving rule: it will force-close any individual foreground application that crosses roughly 4.5GB of active memory usage. Your LLM weights, the vector index, the operating system overhead, and the active text context must all fit comfortably under this 4.5-GB threshold.

This historic “Memory Wall” mandated the use of tiny models (1B-to-3.5B parameters) and short context windows. It also required developers to lean heavily into aggressive flash-memory loading techniques and 4-bit integer quantization to compress model weights without sacrificing output quality.5

The 12-GB Inflection Point: With the release of the Apple A19 Pro architecture, the hardware constraints have fundamentally shifted. The A19 Pro introduces 12GB of LPDDR5X-9600 RAM and an unprecedented peak memory bandwidth of 76.8GB/s.

This is an architectural game-changer for Edge AI. By raising the total system memory to 12GB, the active RAM limit for a foreground application expands significantly. For software architects, this means the 4.5-GB Memory Wall has been shattered.

Financial applications on A19 Pro devices are no longer restricted to 3B-parameter models. Developers can now deploy heavily optimized, highly capable 7B-to-8B-parameter models natively. Furthermore, the 76.8-GB/s bandwidth allows these larger models to stream text at blistering speeds (up to 30-40 tokens per second), and the expanded RAM overhead allows for vastly larger retrieval context windows, enabling the AI to cross-reference multiple years of complex financial data simultaneously.

The Private AI Paradigm

Regardless of the underlying chip, when these engineering constraints are successfully navigated, the resulting system fundamentally transforms the economics and security of financial software.

Because the model weights are downloaded to the device and the MLX inference loop happens entirely locally, the user’s personal financial data never traverses a network. It never hits a load balancer, it is never stored in a server cache, and it is never exposed to a cloud API.

This establishes a true private, sovereign financial ecosystem. The banking institution does not have to worry about data breaches in their AI pipeline because they never take custody of the prompt data. The architecture complies natively with the strictest data protection laws globally because data sovereignty remains unequivocally with the user.

For years, the computing community has treated AI capabilities and user privacy as a zero-sum game. By mastering local RAG and the MLX framework on the mobile edge, we can finally resolve the privacy-utility paradox—delivering uncompromising, intelligent financial advisory with absolute data sovereignty.

item.title: AI Abundance or Luddite Revolution?
item.dc:creator: Peter J. Denning
item.description: Extending unemployment benefits and offering retraining for the new jobs is an affordable safety net for AI-induced job losses.
item.content:encoded:
Will AI lead to massive unemployment? In some sectors, AI is already replacing entry-level jobs.3 Computer science graduates are having increasing difficulty obtaining jobs as AI takes over junior programming jobs. Poorly designed customer-service robots are rapidly displacing customer service agents and forcing customers to submit to a company’s business model. Those whose jobs are being replaced find little comfort in economists’ forecasts that there will eventually be more new jobs than those replaced.

Techno-optimists have advanced “abundance,” a vague hypothesis that AI automation will make most all goods and services so abundant that their costs will be zero and no one will need to work.1 They endorse a universal basic income (UBI) to cover residual costs remaining after abundance zeroes most costs. In the U.S., a common proposal for UBI is $12,000 for every adult, regardless of their economic status.

Techno-pessimists are not persuaded that AI will generate widespread abundance. They believe there will be massive job losses, spread unevenly across sectors and mainly at the entry level. They are worried that mounting job losses will foment social upheaval, with a good chance of violent protests such as in the famous Luddite revolt against automation in the textile industry in 1811–1816. They believe the UBI would not alleviate the angst over loss of work, and its vast expense would provoke a massive economic crisis.

Here we will argue that UBI is not the solution to AI-induced unemployment, and that the sovereign wealth fund (SWF), a popular notion to pay for UBI, will fall far short. We will argue for the much more pragmatic approach of extending unemployment benefits and offering retraining for the new jobs. This approach is affordable, likely to provide a safety net for AI induced job losses, and likely to avoid violent social upheavals.

The Debt Context

Regardless of whether AI automation brings abundance or upheaval, many economies face difficult futures. Government assistance programs are popular and growing but taxes are insufficient to pay for them. This has resulted in large debts exceeding GDP in many countries. The U.S. national debt is $40 trillion (123% of GDP) and growing at more than $2 trillion per year. Several European countries have debts exceeding their GDPs: Greece (146.1%), Italy (137.1%), France (115.6%), Belgium (107.9%), Spain (100.7%) and the UK (100%). Greece and Sweden found the political courage to reduce their national debts, but it was a painful process for politicians and citizens alike. Some pundits argue that AI abundance will improve productivity so much that these countries will eliminate their debts. Given politicians’ proclivity to expand spending rather than shrink debt, that seems like a wishful fantasy. They are ill prepared for disruptions from AI induced unemployment.

Attack of the Luddites

In 1811, British artisans led by Ned Ludd fought back against automated machinery for making textiles by breaking the mechanized looms and knitting frames.a They feared that unskilled machine operators were robbing them of their livelihood.

The Jacquard Loom (1804) accelerated textile automation in the Industrial Revolution. The loom weaved faster than human hands and automated the incorporation of complex patterns into the cloths by storing weaving instructions on punched cards that controlled the movements of the machine. Patterns could be designed in advance and the cards sold to loom holders. Even with automated looms, there was a prosperous “cottage industry” of custom textiles in Europe. No machine could match their workmanship.

Little did the Luddites suspect that, by the time of its peak a century later, the mechanized British textile industry would employ as many as 500,000 workers directly in spinning and weaving. France employed more than two million workers, nearly 40% of its industrial workforce.

Initial experience with the software industry seems to indicate that the new AI coders have impacted mostly entry-level programmers but not senior software developers. Because AI generated codes often contain errors, a new job category is emerging: software verification. The same can be said of other fields, such as accounting or legal services, where new specialists will verify the “work” done by AI.

Over the years, unions formed to oppose automation that did not benefit workers. Modern unions have noted that, since 1980, technology has replaced more U.S. jobs than it has generated.b They are concerned that AI will accelerate this trend.

What Fuels the AI Revolution?

The Industrial Revolution emerged in 17th–19th century Europe and North America. It was supported by capital accumulated through colonialism, trade, and slavery, and relied on energy from coal and oil.2,9,10 By the 19th century, textiles once imported from Asia were increasingly manufactured in Europe using steam-powered machinery and raw materials often produced through slave or low-wage labor. The AI revolution of the 21st century has similar dependencies. Its engines are digital computers powered by electricity generated from fossil fuels, nuclear energy, solar, wind, and water. Its raw materials are data expropriated from artisans or generated by low-wage workers. AI systems are distinguished by four foundational elements:

  • Artificial neural network models, beginning with the McCulloch–Pitts model8 and later probabilistic neuromorphic variants.7

  • Universal function approximation, which enables such models to represent broad classes of mathematical functions.4,6

  • Backpropagation, introduced in 1974 by P.J. Werbos,10 and other gradient-based methods, allowing efficient training of ANNs on large datasets.

  • Large, curated datasets, including text, images, symbols, and other structured information, used to train AI models.

Human labor remains essential. Much of the data used to train AI originates from the work of writers, creators, and data annotators, often receiving little compensation relative to the value they generated. Although hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested in AI infrastructure, far less is spent compensating the people and communities that create and curate the underlying data. A central challenge, therefore, is ensuring that the immense investments driving AI translate into broadly shared economic and social benefits rather than concentrating rewards among a small number of stakeholders. UBI is seen by many as a tool for accomplishing this.

The Jevons Paradox

In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons observed that technological improvements increased the efficiency of coal use and lowered the price of coal, leading to increased demand for coal to run more factories.c AI techno-optimists have latched on to the Jevons paradox to “prove” that AI productivity will increase consumption of AI—the Abundance Hypothesis. Economist Erik Brynjolfsson does not agree that the paradox would apply across the board, because some market segments do not satisfy the conditions for the paradox.3 Nonetheless, entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk predict AI technology will, by 2035, reduce costs to near-zero in all sectors, eliminating the need for employment and rendering money useless.

The UBI

The UBI response to AI employment disruption is that every adult receives a guaranteed income regardless of their economic status. The income does not need to be high because abundance eliminates most costs. Universal basic income proposals often tout a sovereign wealth fund to pay for it.

An example of a successful SWF was established in 2020 by the Seminole Tribe to invest in commercial real estate properties.d The Seminole Tribe owns six casinos, numerous hotels, and the Hard Rock Café, which has restaurants in 74 countries. An Internet post estimates that each adult member of the Seminole Tribe receives $100,000 per year from the fund.e Unfortunately, this example does not generalize to a full population. UBI promoters therefore advocate for a combination of tax overhaul and SWF to generate the funds needed. All the scenarios for collecting enough taxes to pay for UBI imagine a total restructuring of the tax system including confiscatory rates on high earners, annual taxes on wealth including pension funds and stock holdings, value-added tax, a special tax to capture the salary lost when a robot replaces a human, and much higher corporate taxes. There is no way the political system would agree to such massive tax changes. The political system stoutly resists even small reforms to Social Security such as raising retirement age by one year.

The SWF

Because taxation will come up woefully short, the SWF is often proposed to make up the difference. It is basically an investment fund that appreciates along with the stock markets. Some proposers argue that a sufficiently large SWF would gather enough annual interest to cover all the annual UBI payments.

SWFs are state-owned investment funds that manage national wealth through investments in various asset classes such as oil, company stocks, bonds, real estate, and alternative investments like private equity and hedge funds. An AI SWF would have to generate an enormous return on investment (ROI) to support UBI. In the US, the UBI of $12,000 issued annually to 270 million adults would total about $3.2 trillion annually. If the stock market appreciated at X% a year, a SWF with $3.2/X trillion could be self-sustaining. For X=2%, a realistic estimate, the SWF would need $160 trillion. The current U.S. GDP is about $30 trillion and U.S. debt stands at about $40 trillion—so that SWF is approximately five times the GDP.

The SWF estimates here correspond to an economy with the current tax system. The sweeping tax changes noted previously would confiscate so much wealth that the stock market could not function well, and the SWF would collapse.

Other Difficulties

Proponents of UBI often overlook six other difficulties.

The first is the background assumption that everything becomes abundant at about the same rate and the prices of everything keep going down. But the economy is not homogeneous in this way.3 For example, sectors such as solar panel, magnet, and chip manufacturing require rare earths, which are in limited supply worldwide. Robots in those sectors would be unable to achieve “abundance” because of the high costs to obtain the rare earths. Resource limits would affect the abilities of each sector to reduce its unit costs to zero, in many cases producing a floor keeping prices up.

A second difficulty concerns capitalism itself. If products become abundant and consumer prices fall to zero, what incentive remains to start a company? There would be nothing to invest in, no return on investment, and no stocks. Without a stock market, a sovereign wealth fund would have no way to grow. UBI would collapse.

A third difficulty concerns the distributions of human talents. People with greater abilities tend to accumulate more power. Today, that power often becomes wealth. Power is inherently unevenly distributed. Those with more would block acquisition of power by those with less. Those with less would covet those with more. Inequality would worsen rather than disappear. Power struggles would intensify, to no one’s benefit.

A fourth difficulty concerns the value of high skill levels of experts and masters in their fields. People want master physicians to deal with their diseases, master plumbers to repair their pipes, master electricians to install their electricity, master chefs to feed them, and master musicians to inspire them. AI is unlikely to develop skills matching human experts or masters. Those skill levels depend almost entirely on vast reservoirs of tacit knowledge that machines cannot know.5 The humans replaced by machines are likely to be those of lower skill levels, such as beginner or competent levels. If no one is learning the lower skill levels of a domain, who will grow into future experts and masters?

A fifth difficulty is the possibility of inflation erasing the value of UBI. It is commonly proposed that, if the SWF is insufficient, the government can simply print new money to make up the difference. The problem is that “free money” generates inflation. This was demonstrated in the U.S. when the government made massive subsidies available during the COVID pandemic, which stoked a period of high inflation.

A sixth difficulty is the capriciousness of politicians. A recent proposal in the U.S. by Senator Bernie Sanders would confiscate 50% of all the wealth of the large AI companies, currently about $27 trillion. Half that comes nowhere close to funding the SWF needed for the UBI. The one-time confiscation of that wealth would severely impact those companies’ stocks and all the stock market and index funds that depend on them. This shortsighted proposal is unlikely to pass Congress, but the urge behind it to confiscate wealth is growing. A variation on this proposal is for the government to take a stake in many companies, for example 20%, converting that portion of their market value into cash for a SWF.

Conclusion

Will AI lead to a Luddite revolution or will a UBI rescue society when AI takes jobs away from humans? What can governments do? We conclude that a U.S. utopian zero-cost economy is unlikely and the proposed UBI solution funded by SWF investing in the stock market would be far from sufficient to support the American labor force. The UBI proposals overlook that people work not just for a salary but because it gives them purpose and meaning and a sense of contributing to society. Taking away their work takes away their dignity. They feel incomplete and restive.

An alternative is available as a variation of the status quo. Displaced workers would get unemployment benefits until they are employed again. They would be offered retraining in the skill sets of the new jobs. Some jobs could be designated “reserved for humans only.” A tax on AI services would pay for all this.

To us, UBI looks like an infeasible fantasy. There is not enough money, abundance, or popular will to realize a no-work economy. We are in for a rough ride.

item.title: Why Enterprise AI Agents Need Transaction-Level Auditing
item.dc:creator: Rajeshkumar Rajaseakaran Nair
item.description: A five-layer transaction-auditing design offers a practical way to make consequential actions reconstructable, governed, and accountable.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprise AI is moving beyond generating recommendations to initiating business actions. Agents can update customer accounts, change inventory records, approve workflows, and submit payment instructions. Their ability to act creates a practical accountability question: when an agent reports that a task is complete, what evidence establishes that the authorized business outcome actually occurred?

Consider a hypothetical accounts-payable agent instructed to process an approved supplier invoice. It identifies the invoice, calls a payment API, receives a successful acknowledgment, and marks the task complete. Later, the finance team discovers that an outdated supplier mapping directed the payment to an incorrect beneficiary reference. The API performed its operation, but the business objective was not satisfied.

This problem is not unique to AI: distributed enterprise applications have always needed transaction controls and reconciliation. Agentic systems add another decision-making layer between business instructions and application execution. Organizations must be able to reconstruct not only what a service processed, but also why the agent initiated the operation, what authority permitted it, and whether the resulting business state matched the approved request.

Execution Logs Are Not Business Evidence

Application logs can show that a request reached a service, how long it took, and what response the service returned. These observations are essential for operations, but a successful HTTP response does not necessarily mean that a payment settled, an inventory adjustment propagated, or a customer record reached its intended state.

A transaction audit has a different objective from ordinary troubleshooting. It preserves a defensible chain of evidence connecting the original business instruction, authorization decision, executed action, downstream outcome, and final reconciliation. An agent’s generated explanation is useful context, but it should not be the sole authority for determining success.

For consequential actions, the relevant question is not merely “Did the tool call work?” It is, “Can an independent reviewer establish that the action was authorized, traceable, and correct?”

A Five-Layer Architecture for Transaction Accountability

The following five layers are a proposed engineering design pattern for enterprise agent systems, not a formally standardized or experimentally validated framework. They can be implemented using existing identity, workflow, logging, and reconciliation infrastructure.

1. Structured Business Intent

Capture the approved objective before execution in a structured record: operation type, business identifiers, constraints, expected outcome, and reference to the originating request. For a supplier payment, this could include invoice ID, supplier ID, authorized amount, currency, and required settlement condition. A free-form instruction such as “pay the invoice” is insufficient evidence of which transaction was intended.

The system should validate these fields against authoritative sources and minimize unnecessary storage of sensitive prompt content. The intent record becomes the baseline for later comparison.

2. Authorization and Policy Evidence

Enforce permission checks outside the model’s instructions. A trusted policy component should evaluate the requesting identity, agent’s delegated authority, target resource, transaction amount, policy version, and any required human approval.

Capture the authorization decision and its reference before the consequential operation proceeds. This distinguishes an action that was technically possible from one that was actually permitted.

3. Controlled Execution and Event Correlation

Route sensitive operations through controlled interfaces that attach a stable correlation identifier to the business request, authorization decision, tool invocation, and downstream events. A payment workflow may cross an invoice system, supplier master-data service, payment gateway, ledger, and settlement provider, each with different identifiers.

Preserve the mapping among those identifiers. Use idempotency controls where supported, especially when an agent retries after a timeout. An uncertain response must not silently turn into a duplicate payment. Retries and compensating actions should remain visible in the event history.

4. Tamper-Evident Audit Evidence

Preserve consequential events in a durable audit store with appropriate access restrictions and retention rules. Depending on risk and regulatory needs, append-only storage, cryptographic hashes, signatures, and independent administrative controls can help reveal unauthorized modification.

Tamper evidence does not prove that the original data was accurate. A protected but incorrect supplier reference is still incorrect. Evidence provenance, trustworthy source systems, and privacy controls therefore matter as much as storage integrity.

5. Independent Outcome Reconciliation

Use authoritative business records to compare the executed action with the approved intent. A gateway acknowledgment should not be equated with payment settlement. Likewise, a successful inventory API response should not automatically establish consistency with the warehouse ledger.

The reconciliation component should be independent of the agent’s own completion statement. It can use deterministic business rules, authoritative queries, and existing financial or operational controls; it does not require a second AI model.

Transaction states should distinguish accepted, pending, settled, rejected, reversed, and exception conditions as appropriate. An unresolved operation must remain unresolved rather than being forced into a success category.

What a Useful Audit Record Contains

An illustrative payment audit record might look like this. The identifiers and values are fictional, and the example omits production controls such as event timestamps, source attestations, and access metadata.

{
  "transaction_id": "TXN-10482",
  "correlation_id": "CORR-88291",
  "agent_id": "AP-AGENT-07",
  "invoice_id": "INV-2048",
  "supplier_id": "SUP-102",
  "approved_amount": 18500,
  "currency": "USD",
  "authorization": {"decision": "APPROVED", "policy_version": "3.2"},
  "execution": {"status": "ACCEPTED", "payment_ref": "PAY-7782"},
  "outcome": {"settlement": "PENDING", "reconciliation": "OPEN"}

Following a Supplier Payment Through the Evidence

Suppose an approved invoice requires an $18,500 payment to Supplier A. The agent submits the correct amount, but an outdated mapping supplies an incorrect beneficiary reference. The gateway accepts the request. An execution-only dashboard may show green.

The structured intent identifies the approved supplier and invoice. Authorization evidence establishes the scope of the agent’s permission. Execution evidence records the actual beneficiary reference submitted to the payment service. Reconciliation compares that reference and any resulting settlement information with authoritative supplier and finance records.

If the records disagree, the system flags an exception and alerts an authorized operations team. Where possible, the organization may intervene before settlement; otherwise the evidence supports investigation and remediation. Auditing cannot prevent every error, but it can make the error detectable, attributable, and actionable.

Designing for Distributed and Incomplete Outcomes

Agent-initiated transactions often span asynchronous systems. Events may arrive late or out of order, and downstream applications may become consistent only after a delay. Audit services should preserve event time, processing time, source identity, and links between original and compensating transactions.

Reconciliation deadlines should reflect business reality. A delayed settlement notice is not necessarily a failed payment, but it is also not proof of success. A reliable audit architecture explicitly represents uncertainty and escalates exceptions when evidence is missing or a verification deadline expires.

Operational Measures and Trade-Offs

Organizations can assess the auditing capability through measures such as the share of consequential agent actions with complete evidence, unreconciled transaction volume, reconciliation latency, duplicate execution attempts, policy exceptions, and investigation time.

Engineering teams should test the audit system with missing events, delayed responses, conflicting records, and retries. These tests reveal whether the system preserves the distinction between technical execution and verified business completion under failure conditions.

Implementation also involves trade-offs. Synchronous checks can increase latency; asynchronous reconciliation can delay final confirmation. Audit records require privacy safeguards, data minimization, restricted access, and retention policies. Ownership of exceptions must be defined across engineering, business operations, security, and compliance.

Trust Requires Verifiable Business Evidence

As AI agents acquire authority to change consequential enterprise records, the standard for trustworthy operation must extend beyond successful tool invocation. Organizations need evidence that connects business intent, authorization, execution, and independently verified outcome.

A five-layer transaction-auditing design offers one practical way to establish that connection. Its purpose is not to eliminate autonomy, but to make consequential actions reconstructable, governed, and accountable. The central question for enterprise AI is no longer only whether an agent can complete a task. It is whether the enterprise can establish, from independent evidence, that the right transaction was completed.

Rajeshkumar Rajaseakaran Nair is a Test Specialist at IBM Corporation with more than nineteen years of experience in enterprise software quality engineering and validation across retail and telecommunications systems. An IEEE Senior Member and ACM Professional Member, his interests include AI validation engineering, software reliability, and trustworthy enterprise AI systems.
